On locally nilpotent derivations of polynomial algebra in three variables

Nikhilesh Dasgupta* Affiliation: *Department of Mathematics, Affiliation: Gandhi Institute of Technology and Management (GITAM) University, Affiliation: Bengaluru, Karnataka 561203, India. Affiliation: e-mail: its.nikhilesh@gmail.com, ndasgupt@gitam.edu    Sergey Gaifullin† Affiliation: †Faculty of Computer Science, Affiliation: HSE University, Affiliation: Pokrovsky Boulevard 11, Moscow 109028, Russia. Affiliation: e-mail: sgayf@yandex.ru
Abstract

In this paper we investigate locally nilpotent derivations on the polynomial algebra in three variables over a field of characteristic zero. We introduce an iterating construction giving all locally nilpotent derivations of rank 22. This construction allows to get examples of non-triangularizable locally nilpotent derivations of rank 22. We also show that the well-known example of a locally nilpotent derivation of rank 33, given by Freudenburg, is a member of a large family of new examples of rank 33 locally nilpotent derivations. Our approach is based on considering all locally nilpotent derivations commuting with a given one. We obtain a characterization of locally nilpotent derivations with a given rank in terms of sets of commuting locally nilpotent derivations.

Keywords. Polynomial ring, locally nilpotent derivation, rank, kernel, triangularizable derivation.

2020 MSC. Primary: 14R10, 14R20; Secondary: 13A50, 32M17.

1 Introduction

By a ring, we mean a Noetherian ring with unity. Let kk be a field of characteristic zero and BB be a kk-algebra. We use the notation B=k[n]B=k^{[n]} to denote that BB is isomorphic to the polynomial algebra in nn variables over kk. A kk-linear map δ:B→B\delta:B\rightarrow B is said to be a kk-derivation if it satisfies the Leibnitz rule: δ⁡(a​b)=a​δ​(b)+b​δ​(a)\delta(ab)=a\delta(b)+b\delta(a) for all a,b∈Ba,b\in B. A kk-derivation δ\delta is a said to be a locally nilpotent derivation (abbrev. LND) if, for each b∈Bb\in B, there exits n⁡(b)∈ℕn(b)\in\mathbb{N} such that δn⁡(b)​(b)=0\delta^{n(b)}(b)=0. The BB-subalgebra A:={b∈B|δ⁡(b)=0}A:=\{b\in B~|~\delta(b)=0\} is called the kernel of δ\delta and denoted by Ker​δ{\rm Ker}~\delta. The set of all LNDs of BB is denoted by LND⁡(B){\rm LND}(B).

When kk is algebraically closed, the group of regular automorphisms Aut⁡(k[n])\mathrm{Aut}(k^{[n]}) is a classical object of investigation in affine algebraic geometry. There are a lot of famous long standing problems about Aut⁡(k[n])\mathrm{Aut}(k^{[n]}) such as Jacobian conjecture, Linearization problem, Tameness problem and so on. One of the approaches to study Aut⁡(k[n])\mathrm{Aut}(k^{[n]}) is to study all algebraic subgroups in it. Each connected linear algebraic group is generated by one-dimensional subgroups isomorphic to the additive or the multiplicative group of kk. We call such subgroups 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a} and 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-subgroups, respectively. The 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-subgroups correspond to locally nilpotent derivations of k[n]k^{[n]}.

LNDs became a powerful tool for investigating kk-algebras. In 1996, Makar-Limanov [22] introduced a new invariant of a kk-algebra BB, which was later named the Makar-Limanov invariant. It is the intersection of kernels of all LNDs on BB and is denoted by ML⁡(B){\rm ML}(B). This invariant allows one to prove that the Koras-Russell cubic {x+x2y+z2+t3=0}\{x+x^{2}y+z^{2}+t^{3}=0\} is not isomorphic to the three dimensional affine space. Generalization of this result given by Kaliman and Makar-Limanov in 1997 was the final step in the proof of the Linearization problem for ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action on ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3} [21]. One can also use ML⁡(B){\rm ML}(B) for the purpose of describing all automorphisms of a kk-algebra BB [23, 25, 27, 14]. In [13], characterizations of k[2]k^{[2]} and k[3]k^{[3]} in terms of the Makar-Limanov invariant are obtained.

Another popular concept based on the concept of LNDs is that of flexibility of an affine algebraic variety. Let SAut⁡(X)\mathrm{SAut}(X) denote the group generated by all 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-subgroups in Aut⁡(k⁡[X])\mathrm{Aut}(k[X]), where k⁡[X]k[X] is the algebra of regular functions on an affine algebraic variety XX. In [1] it is proved that if SAut⁡(X)\mathrm{SAut}(X) acts on the regular locus Xr​e​gX^{reg} transitively, then it acts on Xr​e​gX^{reg} infinitely transitively, i.e. every mm-tuple {a1,…,am}\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}\} of distinct points in Xr​e​gX^{reg} can be moved to any mm-tuple {b1,…,bm}\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{m}\} of distinct points in Xr​e​gX^{reg} by an element of SAut⁡(X)\mathrm{SAut}(X). Such varieties are called flexible. It turns out that many natural classes of varieties including affine spaces are flexible [2, 1, 15, 28].

Although LNDs are popular objects of investigation, even for many well-known algebras it is a complicated problem to describe all LNDs on these algebras. For example, in case of the polynomial algebra k[n]k^{[n]}, there is no complete description starting from n=3n=3. For n=1n=1, each LND of k⁡[x]k[x] has the form c​∂∂xc\frac{\partial}{\partial x}, where c∈kc\in k. For n=2n=2, each LND of k⁡[x,y]k[x,y] has the form f⁡(u)​∂∂vf(u)\frac{\partial}{\partial v}, where {u,v}\{u,v\} is a coordinate system of k[2]k^{[2]}, i.e. k⁡[x,y]=k⁡[u,v]k[x,y]=k[u,v] (Theorem 2.7). When n⩾3n\geqslant 3, there is no such explicit description of an arbitrary LND, but there are many known examples. Indeed, each triangularizable derivation is an LND. By a triangularizable derivation, we mean a derivation δ\delta on k[n]k^{[n]} such that in some coordinate system {x1,…,xn}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\} we have δ⁡(xi)∈k⁡[x1,…,xi−1]\delta(x_{i})\in k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1}], in particular, δ⁡(x1)∈k\delta(x_{1})\in k. For n=3n=3, there exists a complete description of LNDs which contain at least one variable in its kernel, given by Daigle and Freudenburg (Theorem 2.18). It seems that starting from n=4n=4 the situation becomes very difficult. An important technique to study an LND is by investigating its kernel. Indeed, it is easy to see that for n⩽2n\leqslant 2 the kernel of any non-zero LND of k[n]k^{[n]} is a polynomial ring. For n=3n=3, this fact is the statement of Miyanishi’s theorem [19, Theorem 5.1]. But for n⩾5n\geqslant 5 the kernel of an LND can be even non finitely generated [11]. For n=4n=4, though it is known that the kernel of an LND is finitely generated if it annihilates a variable [3, Theorem 1] and is also a polynomial ring if in addition, the kernel is regular [4], the question of finite generation of the kernel remains open in general. That is why our paper is devoted to the case n=3n=3. This paper is an attempt to understand how do LNDs on k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z] look like.

If δ\delta is an LND and h∈Ker​δh\in\mathrm{Ker}\,\delta, then h​δh\delta is also an LND, which is called a replica of δ\delta. So, to investigate all LNDs in some sense it is sufficient to investigate irreducible ones, i.e. LNDs whose image is not contained in any non-trivial principal ideal. Indeed, all LNDs are replicas of irreducible ones. Each derivation of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] has the form

δ=f1​∂∂x1+…+fn​∂∂xn,wherefi∈k⁡[x1,…,xn].\delta=f_{1}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}+\ldots+f_{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}},\qquad\text{where}\quad f_{i}\in k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}].

If we change the system of coordinates, i.e. consider such y1,…,yny_{1},\ldots,y_{n} that k⁡[y1,…,yn]=k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}]=k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], then δ\delta has the form

f~1​∂∂y1+…+f~n​∂∂yn,f~i∈k⁡[y1,…,yn].\widetilde{f}_{1}\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{1}}+\ldots+\widetilde{f}_{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{n}},\qquad\widetilde{f}_{i}\in k[y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}].

The minimal number of non-zero f~1,…,f~n\widetilde{f}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{f}_{n} for various systems of coordinates is called rank of the derivation δ\delta, denoted by rk​δ\mathrm{rk}~\delta. If rk​δ=0\mathrm{rk}\,\delta=0, then δ=0\delta=0. Every LND of rank 11 is a replica of the derivation ∂∂x1\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}} in some coordinate system {x1,…,xn}\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\} of k[n]k^{[n]} (Proposition 2.12). It is easy to prove that a replica of a triangularizable derivation has rank at most n−1n-1. But the converse is not true even for n=3n=3. On k[3]k^{[3]}, there are examples of non-triangularizable irreducible LNDs of rank 2. The first example of a non-triangularizable LND of k[3]k^{[3]} was given by Bass [5], which was generalized to k[n]k^{[n]} for n⩾4n\geqslant 4 by Popov [29]. More examples were given by Freudenburg [16, Example 2] and Daigle [8, Example 3.5]. Later, Freudenburg [18] proved that there exist LNDs on k[3]k^{[3]} of rank 33. This example of Freudenburg (see Section 5) is given by some rather complicated polynomials. The proof that this LND is of rank 33, is based on the fact that it is homogeneous with respect to a ℤ\mathbb{Z}-grading on BB. Later, he introduced the technique of local slice constructions [17] to generalize this example and obtained new examples of rank 33 LNDs. Similar examples were also obtained by Daigle, who used a geometric approach. The connection between his geometric approach and local slice constructions is described in [9]. Although the local slice construction itself does not require any kind of homogeneity, the earlier examples of rank 33 LNDs obtained by these methods were all homogeneous with respect to some positive ℤ\mathbb{Z} gradings.

Our approach to studying LNDs of k[3]k^{[3]} is based on investigating all LNDs that commute with a fixed one. It is easy to see that, given any LND δ\delta, all LNDs equivalent to δ\delta commute with δ\delta. Recall that, two LNDs are called equivalent if their kernels coincide. We prove the following characterization of irreducible LNDs of rank 33: an irreducible LND δ\delta of k[3]k^{[3]} has rank 3 if and only if every LND commuting with it is equivalent to δ\delta (see Theorem 4.5). Note that, for a reducible LND, it is not true. We give an explicit criterion for an LND to have a non-equivalent commuting one (see Proposition 4.1). It allows us to construct LNDs even of rank 11 without non-equivalent commuting ones. For example, one can consider the derivation x​y​∂∂zxy\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} on k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z]. We also prove that each LND of k[3]k^{[3]} can be restricted to a canonical (possibly, proper) subalgebra of k[3]k^{[3]} isomorphic to k[3]k^{[3]}, such that the restriction is an LND of rank one. We prove that if a restriction of an irreducible LND has no non-equivalent commuting LNDs then the initial LND δ\delta also has no non-equivalent commuting LNDs and hence has rank 33 (Remark 5.2 and Proposition 5.4). This allows us to prove a sufficient condition when a local slice construction gives an LND of rank 3 (Corollary 5.6). So, we obtain a new proof that Freudenburg’s example is of rank 33 and construct new non-homogeneous examples of rank 33 LNDs (Theorem 5.7).

In this paper, we develop a new technique to obtain new LNDs via chains of commuting LNDs starting form basic partial derivations. We prove that every irreducible LND on k[n]k^{[n]} of rank at most 22 can be obtained by an iterative construction from partial derivations in some coordinate system (Corollary 3.18). We call this construction as the Modified Commuting LND Construction (abbrev. MC-construction). It has a close connection with amalgamated product structure of Aut⁡(k[2])\mathrm{Aut}(k^{[2]}). The minimal number of steps of this construction is defined to be the level of the LND. This gives a new numerical characteristic, which shows how complicated the LND is. The simplest LNDs of rank at most 22 are LNDs of rank 11, then come the triangularizable LNDs. As the level of an LND depends on the choice of coordinate system, one can take the minimum over a suitable collection of coordinate systems. That minimum number is called the universal level of DD. We show that an LND has rank 11 if and only if it has universal level 11 and it is triangularizable if and only if it has universal level 33 (Theorem 3.20). In our definition, no LND has universal level 22. Using the MC-construction technique, we construct a new family of non-triangularizable LNDs of rank 2 (Example 4.14). These examples are different from the earlier examples of Freudenburg [16] and Daigle [8]. In a forthcoming paper, we will give a description of the isotropy subgroup of an LND of k[3]k^{[3]}, i.e. the subgroup of Aut⁡(k[3]){\rm Aut}(k^{[3]}) consisting of all automorphisms of k[3]k^{[3]} commuting with this LND.

2 Preliminaries

For a ring RR, we denote the multiplicative group of units by R∗R^{*}. Let k[n]k^{[n]} be the polynomial ring in nn variables over kk. We say that 𝐱={x1,…,xn}\mathbf{x}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}, xi∈k[n]x_{i}\in k^{[n]} is a coordinate system or system of variables if k[n]=k⁡[x1,…,xn]k^{[n]}=k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. By a coordinate or a variable we mean such an element that it can be included in a coordinate system. If α\alpha is an automorphism of k[n]k^{[n]} such that α⁡(xi)=fi\alpha(x_{i})=f_{i}, then we use the notation α=(f1,…,fn)\alpha=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}).

Definition 2.1.

For a coordinate system 𝐱={x1,…,xn}\mathbf{x}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\} of k[n]k^{[n]}, an automorphsim α=(f1,…,fn)\alpha=(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}) is said to be triangular if fi∈k⁡[x1,…,xi]f_{i}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{i}] for each ii, 1⩽i⩽n1\leqslant i\leqslant n. We denote the subgroup of triangular automorphisms by Tn​(k,𝐱){\rm T}_{n}(k;\mathbf{x}) or more simply by Tn​(k){\rm T}_{n}(k) when the coordinate system 𝐱\mathbf{x} is understood from the context. The subgroup of Aut⁡(k[n]){\rm Aut}(k^{[n]}) generated by GLn​(k){\rm GL}_{n}(k) and the triangular automorphisms is called the tame subgroup relative to the coordinate system 𝐱\mathbf{x}, and is denoted by TAn​(k,𝐱){\rm TA}_{n}(k;\mathbf{x}).

It is well-known that every automorphism of k[2]k^{[2]} is tame. This result was first proved by Jung [20] for characteristic zero and generalized to arbitrary characteristic by Van der Kulk [31]. The next theorem gives the explicit structure of Aut⁡(k[2]){\rm Aut}(k^{[2]}) [19, Theorem 4.2]. Though this result was initially contained in the works of Van der Kulk, it was Nagata who stated and proved it in this exact form [26]. His proof assumed kk to be algebraically closed. Later, in his Ph.D. thesis, Wright proved this theorem for the general case [32].

Theorem 2.2.

Let kk be any field. Then Aut⁡(k[2]){\rm Aut}(k^{[2]}) has the structure of an amalgamated free product. More precisely,

Aut⁡(k[2])=Af2​(k)∗CT2​(k),{\rm Aut}(k^{[2]})={\rm Af}_{2}(k)\ast_{C}{\rm T}_{2}(k),

where Af2​(k){\rm Af}_{2}(k) is the subgroup of affine automorphisms

Af2(k)={(xy)↦(a11​x+a12​y+b1a21​x+a22​y+b2)|(a11a12a21a22)∈GL2(k)andb1,b2∈k}.\rm{Af}_{2}(k)=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}x+a_{12}y+b_{1}\\ a_{21}x+a_{22}y+b_{2}\end{pmatrix}\Big|\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}\\ a_{21}&a_{22}\end{pmatrix}\in{\rm GL}_{2}(k)~\text{and}~b_{1},b_{2}\in k\ \right\}.

and C:=Af2​(k)∩T2​(k)C:={\rm Af}_{2}(k)\cap{\rm T}_{2}(k).

Let us recall some basic facts about locally nilpotent derivations. A detailed treatise in this field can be found in the book by Freudenburg [19]. Let BB be an affine kk-domain. The set of all LNDs of BB we denote by LND⁡(B){\rm LND}(B). Each LND DD induces a degree function degD:B∖{0}→ℤ⩾0\deg_{D}\colon B\setminus\{0\}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}, given by

degD⁡f:=m,where​Dm​(f)≠0​and​Dm+1​(f)=0.\deg_{D}\,f:=m,~\text{where}~D^{m}(f)\neq 0~\text{and}~D^{m+1}(f)=0.

This degree function satisfies the usual properties of a degree function:

  1. (i)

    degD⁡(f+g)⩽max⁡{degD⁡f,degD⁡g}\deg_{D}(f+g)\leqslant\mathrm{max}\{\deg_{D}\,f,\deg_{D}\,g\};

  2. (ii)

    degD⁡(f​g)=degD⁡f+degD⁡g\deg_{D}(fg)=\deg_{D}\,f+\deg_{D}\,g.

For each non-zero LND DD its kernel A=Ker​DA=\mathrm{Ker}\,D is a factorially closed subalgebra such that the transcendence degree of BB over AA equals 1, see [19, Principle 1]. Recall that, a subalgebra AA of an algebra BB is said to be factorially closed in BB, if for any a,b∈Ba,b\in B, the condition a​b∈Aab\in A implies that both aa and bb are in AA. If S⊂A∖{0}S\subset A\setminus\{0\} is multiplicatively closed, then DD induces an LND on S−1​BS^{-1}B with kernel S−1​AS^{-1}A, see [19, Principle 9].

Definition 2.3.

Let BB be a kk-algebra. We say two locally nilpotent derivations D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} of BB to be equivalent if Ker​D1=Ker​D2{\rm Ker}~D_{1}={\rm Ker}~D_{2}.

It is well-known that two non-zero LNDs D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} are equivalent if and only if there exist non-zero a,b∈Ba,b\in B such that a​D1=b​D2aD_{1}=bD_{2}. It is easy to see that both aa and bb can be chosen in Ker​D1=Ker​D2{\rm Ker}~D_{1}={\rm Ker}~D_{2}, see [19, Principle 12].

Definition 2.4.

Let D∈LND⁡(B)D\in{\rm LND}(B). An element s∈Bs\in B is called a slice if D​s=1Ds=1, and a local slice if D​s∈Ker​DDs\in{\rm Ker}D and D​s≠0Ds\neq 0, i.e., degD​(s)=1{\rm deg}_{D}(s)=1.

A local slice exists for every non-zero LND. But the existence of a slice is a rather strict condition for an LND. The following important result is known as the Slice Theorem, see [19, Corollary 1.26].

Theorem 2.5.

Let BB a kk-domain. Suppose D∈LND⁡(B)D\in{\rm LND}(B) admits a slice s∈Bs\in B, and let A=Ker​DA={\rm Ker}~D. Then B=A⁡[s]B=A[s] and D=∂∂sD=\frac{\partial}{\partial s}.

The following assertion, see [19, Principle 11(d)], is a generalization of the above theorem.

Proposition 2.6.

Let rr be a local slice of DD. Then the following holds B​[1D⁡(r)]=A​[1D⁡(r)]​[r]B\left[\frac{1}{D(r)}\right]=A\left[\frac{1}{D(r)}\right][r].

Now we assume B=k[n]B=k^{[n]}. We start with the result, due to Rentschler [30], which characterizes all locally nilpotent derivations on k[2]k^{[2]}.

Theorem 2.7.

Let DD be a non-zero LND of k⁡[x,y]k[x,y]. There there exists a tame automorphism α∈T​A2​(k,{x,y})\alpha\in TA_{2}(k;\{x,y\}) and p⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]p(x)\in k[x] such that α​D​α−1=p⁡(x)​∂∂y.\alpha D{\alpha}^{-1}=p(x)\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}.

In particular, it follows from this theorem that the kernel of any non-zero LND of k[2]k^{[2]} is isomorphic to k[1]k^{[1]}. The next theorem is a famous result of Miyanishi which gives the structure of the kernel of any non-zero LND on k[3]k^{[3]}, see [19, Theorem 5.1].

Theorem 2.8.

Let D(≠0)∈LND⁡(k[3])D(\neq 0)\in{\rm LND}(k^{[3]}). Then Ker​D≅k[2]{\rm Ker}~D\cong k^{[2]}.

Definition 2.9.

The rank of DD, denoted by rk​D\mathrm{rk}\,D, is defined to be the least integer ii for which there exists a coordinate system {x1,x2,…,xn}\{x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}\} of BB satisfying

k⁡[xi+1,…,xn]⊆Ker​D.k[x_{i+1},\dots,x_{n}]\subseteq\mathrm{Ker}\,D.

It is easy to see that this definition is equivalent to the definition of rank given in the introduction. If rk​D=0\mathrm{rk}\,D=0, then D=0D=0. So, for any non-zero LND DD, 1⩽rk​D⩽n1\leqslant\mathrm{rk}\,D\leqslant n.

Let BB be an affine kk-domain and D∈LND⁡(B)D\in{\rm LND}(B) with the kernel AA and the image D​BDB. It can be proved that the intersection of the kernel and the image A∩D​BA\cap DB is an ideal in AA. It is called plinth ideal and is denoted by pl⁡(D)\mathrm{pl}(D). The following result called the Plinth Ideal Theorem follows from the works of Bonnet [7] and Daigle-Kaliman [12].

Theorem 2.10.

Let B=k[3]B=k^{[3]}, D∈LND⁡(B)D\in{\rm LND}(B) and A=Ker​DA={\rm Ker}~D. Then the following hold:

  1. (i)

    BB is a faithfully flat AA-module;

  2. (ii)

    the plinth ideal pl⁡(D)\mathrm{pl}(D) is principal.

Definition 2.11.

Let B=k[3]B=k^{[3]}, D∈LND⁡(B)D\in{\rm LND}(B). A local slice rr is called a minimal local slice of DD if D⁡(r)D(r) is a generator of the plinth ideal A∩D​BA\cap DB.

The following result due to Freudenburg characterizes rank 11 LNDs of k[n]k^{[n]}, see [16].

Proposition 2.12.

Up to a change of coordinates, every locally nilpotent derivation DD of r​a​n​k​1rank~1 on k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is of the form D=h​∂∂xnD=h\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}} where h∈k⁡[x1,…,xn−1]h\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1}].

We next state an important result on the intersection of kernels of LNDs of k[3]k^{[3]} [19, Theorem 5.13].

Theorem 2.13.

Let D1,D2∈LND⁡(k[3])D_{1},D_{2}\in{\rm LND}(k^{[3]}). Then exactly one of the following statements holds:

  1. (i)

    Ker​D1∩Ker​D2=k{\rm Ker}~D_{1}\cap{\rm Ker}~D_{2}=k;

  2. (ii)

    there exist f,g,h∈Bf,g,h\in B such that Ker​D1=k⁡[f,g]{\rm Ker}~D_{1}=k[f,g], Ker​D2=k⁡[f,h]{\rm Ker}~D_{2}=k[f,h] and Ker​D1∩Ker​D2=k⁡[f]{\rm Ker}~D_{1}\cap{\rm Ker}~D_{2}=k[f];

  3. (iii)

    Ker​D1=Ker​D2{\rm Ker}~D_{1}={\rm Ker}~D_{2}.

We are particularly interested in the case when two LNDs commute. The next result due to Daigle and Kaliman [19, Theorem 3] describes the intersection of kernels of two commuting non-equivalent LNDs of k[3]k^{[3]}. It was earlier observed by Maubach [24, Theorem 3.6] for k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}.

Proposition 2.14.

If D,E∈LND⁡(k[3])D,E\in{\rm LND}(k^{[3]}) are non-zero, commuting and have distinct kernels, then there exists a variable f∈k[3]f\in k^{[3]} such that Ker​D∩Ker​E=k⁡[f]{\rm Ker}~D\cap{\rm Ker}~E=k[f].

The following result involving local slices of LNDs on k[3]k^{[3]} is due to Daigle [10, Lemma 2.5].

Lemma 2.15.

Let B=k[3]B=k^{[3]}, D(≠0)∈LND⁡(B)D(\neq 0)\in{\rm LND}(B), A:=Ker​DA:={\rm Ker}~D and f∈Af\in A. Then the following hold:

  1. (i)

    if ff is a variable of BB, then it is a variable of AA;

  2. (ii)

    if ff is a variable of AA and there exists g∈Bg\in B such that D⁡(g)∈k⁡[f]∖{0}D(g)\in k[f]\setminus\{0\}, then ff is a variable of BB.

The next result due to Freudenburg [16, Proposition 1] is called the Restriction /extension principle.

Proposition 2.16.

Let D∈LND⁡(k⁡[x1,…,xn])D\in{\rm LND}(k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]). If DD restricts to a derivation on k⁡[x1,…,xn−1]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1}]. Then D​xn∈k⁡[x1,…,xn−1]Dx_{n}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1}].

Now let us consider the polynomial ring in nn variables R[n]R^{[n]} over a ring RR. By an RR-derivation, we mean a derivation vanishing on RR. If we are given n−1n-1 polynomials f1,…,fn−1f_{1},\ldots,f_{n-1}, we can consider the Jacobian derivation δ=Jac(f1,…,fn−1,⋅)\delta={\rm Jac}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n-1},\cdot) such that

δ⁡(h)=Jac⁡(f1,…,fn−1,h)=detJ⁡(f1,…,fn−1,h),\delta(h)={\rm Jac}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n-1},h)=\det J(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n-1},h),

where JJ is the Jacobian matrix. The Jacobian derivation is always an RR-derivation, but it is not always locally nilpotent.

Let us recall the concept of local slice construction introduced in [17]. Put B=k[3]B=k^{[3]}. Suppose D∈LND⁡(B)D\in\mathrm{LND}(B) is irredducible and there exist such f,g,r∈Bf,g,r\in B, r∉g​Br\notin gB and P∈k[1]P\in k^{[1]} that Ker​D=k⁡[f,g]\mathrm{Ker}\,D=k[f,g] and D⁡(r)=g​P​(f)≠0D(r)=gP(f)\neq 0. Then there exists ϕ∈k​[f][1]\phi\in k[f]^{[1]} such that ϕ⁡(r)∈g​B\phi(r)\in gB. We assume ϕ\phi to be of minimal rr degree with such property. Also assume ϕ⁡(r)\phi(r) to be irreducible in k⁡[f,r]k[f,r]. Denote h=ϕ⁡(f)​g−1∈Bh=\phi(f)g^{-1}\in B.

Theorem 2.17.

[17, Theorem 2]

(a) Δ=Jac(f,h,⋅)\Delta={\rm Jac}(f,h,\cdot) is an LND of BB;

(b) Δ⁡(r)=−h​P​(f)\Delta(r)=-hP(f);

(c) If Δ\Delta is irreducible, then Ker​Δ=k⁡[f,h]\mathrm{Ker}\,\Delta=k[f,h].

We say that Δ\Delta is obtained from DD by a local slice construction from the data (f,g,r)(f,g,r).

We end this section by stating a theorem of Daigle and Freudenburg which characterizes all RR-LNDs of R[2]R^{[2]}, where RR is a UFD containing ℚ\mathbb{Q} [11, Theorem 2.4].

Theorem 2.18.

Let RR be a UFD containing ℚ\mathbb{Q} with field of fractions KK and let B=R⁡[x,y]=R[2]B=R[x,y]=R^{[2]}. For an RR-derivation D≠0D\neq 0 of BB, the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    DD is locally nilpotent;

  2. (ii)

    D=α​Jac​(F,⋅)D=\alpha{\rm Jac}(F,\cdot), for some F∈BF\in B which is a variable of K⁡[x,y]K[x,y] satisfying
    g​c​dB​(∂F∂x,∂F∂y)=1gcd_{B}(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x},\frac{\partial F}{\partial y})=1, and for some α∈R⁡[F]∖{0}\alpha\in R[F]\setminus\{0\}.

Moreover, if the above conditions are satisfied, then K​e​rKer D=R⁡[F]=R[1]D=R[F]=R^{[1]}.

3 Commuting LND Construction

Let BB be an affine kk-domain and D1,D2∈LND⁡(B)D_{1},D_{2}\in{\rm LND}(B). One may ask whether the derivation D1+D2D_{1}+D_{2} is also an LND. In general, it is not true but the answer is affirmative when D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} commute. However, this property does not hold for replicas of LNDs, i.e., if we have two commuting LNDs, the sum of their replicas may not be locally nilpotent.

Example 3.1.

Consider two commuting LNDs ∂∂x\frac{\partial}{\partial x} and ∂∂y\frac{\partial}{\partial y} of k⁡[x,y]k[x,y]. The sum of their replicas y​∂∂x+x​∂∂yy\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+x\frac{\partial}{\partial y} is not locally nilpotent.

The following lemma shows that if we take replicas of a special form, then their sum is an LND.

Lemma 3.2.

Let BB be an affine kk-domain and δ1,…,δm∈LND⁡(B)\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{m}\in{\rm LND}(B) be non-zero and pairwise commuting, i.e., δi​δj=δj​δi\delta_{i}\delta_{j}=\delta_{j}\delta_{i} for all i,j∈{1,…,m}i,j\in\{1,\dots,m\}. Suppose

fk∈⋂i=kmKer​δi,1⩽k⩽m.f_{k}\in\bigcap_{i=k}^{m}{\rm Ker}~\delta_{i},~~~1\leqslant k\leqslant m.

Then Δ=∑i=1nfi​δi\Delta=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}\delta_{i} is an LND of BB.

Proof.

It is easy to see that Δ\Delta is a derivation of BB. So it is enough to check that it is locally nilpotent. Let us fix g∈Bg\in B. We define inductively positive integers ljl_{j} from j=1j=1 to j=mj=m by lj=degδj​(g​∏i=j+1mfili)+1l_{j}={\rm deg}_{\delta_{j}}\left(g\prod_{i=j+1}^{m}f_{i}^{l_{i}}\right)+1. fa1​δa1∘…∘fae​δae​(g)=0.f_{a_{1}}\delta_{a_{1}}\circ\ldots\circ f_{a_{e}}\delta_{a_{e}}(g)=0.

Indeed, if mm occurs among a1,…,aea_{1},\ldots,a_{e} at least lml_{m} times, then since δm\delta_{m} commutes with fif_{i} and δi\delta_{i} we have for some ψ\psi:

fa1​δa1∘…∘fae​δae​(g)=ψ∘δmlm​(g)=0.f_{a_{1}}\delta_{a_{1}}\circ\ldots\circ f_{a_{e}}\delta_{a_{e}}(g)=\psi\circ\delta_{m}^{l_{m}}(g)=0.

Note, that δm−1\delta_{m-1} commutes with all fif_{i} and δi\delta_{i}, except fmf_{m}. If mm occurs among a1,…,aea_{1},\ldots,a_{e} less than lml_{m} times and m−1m-1 occurs among a1,…,aea_{1},\ldots,a_{e} at least lm−1l_{m-1} times, then we have for some ψ\psi:

fa1​δa1∘…∘fae​δae​(g)=ψ∘δm−1b1​fmc1∘…∘δm−1bt​fmct∘δm−1bt+1​(g),f_{a_{1}}\delta_{a_{1}}\circ\ldots\circ f_{a_{e}}\delta_{a_{e}}(g)=\psi\circ\delta_{m-1}^{b_{1}}f_{m}^{c_{1}}\circ\ldots\circ\delta_{m-1}^{b_{t}}f_{m}^{c_{t}}\circ\delta_{m-1}^{b_{t+1}}(g),

where ∑i=1t+1bi⩾lm−1\sum\limits_{i=1}^{t+1}b_{i}\geqslant l_{m-1}, ∑i=1tci<lm\sum\limits_{i=1}^{t}c_{i}<l_{m}. We have

degδm−1⁡(δm−1b1​fmc1∘…∘δm−1bt​fmct∘δm−1bt+1​(g))⩽degδm−1⁡(g​fmlm)−lm−1<0.\deg_{\delta_{m-1}}\left(\delta_{m-1}^{b_{1}}f_{m}^{c_{1}}\circ\ldots\circ\delta_{m-1}^{b_{t}}f_{m}^{c_{t}}\circ\delta_{m-1}^{b_{t+1}}(g)\right)\leqslant\deg_{\delta_{m-1}}\left(gf_{m}^{l_{m}}\right)-l_{m-1}<0.

This means that δm−1b1​fmc1∘…∘δm−1bt​fmct∘δm−1bt+1​(g)=0\delta_{m-1}^{b_{1}}f_{m}^{c_{1}}\circ\ldots\circ\delta_{m-1}^{b_{t}}f_{m}^{c_{t}}\circ\delta_{m-1}^{b_{t+1}}(g)=0.

Similarly we can consider cases when ii occurs among a1,…,aea_{1},\ldots,a_{e} less than lil_{i} times for all i>ji>j and jj occurs among a1,…,asa_{1},\ldots,a_{s} at least lil_{i} times. In all these cases we have

fa1​δa1∘…∘fae​δae​(g)=0.f_{a_{1}}\delta_{a_{1}}\circ\ldots\circ f_{a_{e}}\delta_{a_{e}}(g)=0.

But since e>∑i=1m(li−1)e>\sum\limits_{i=1}^{m}(l_{i}-1), we are in one of these cases.

If we expand Δe​(g)\Delta^{e}(g), we obtain a sum of expressions fa1​δa1∘…∘fae​δae​(g)f_{a_{1}}\delta_{a_{1}}\circ\ldots\circ f_{a_{e}}\delta_{a_{e}}(g). Therefore, Δe​(g)=0\Delta^{e}(g)=0. ∎

Definition 3.3.

We say that Δ\Delta in Lemma 3.2, is obtained by a Commuting LND Construction (denoted by CC-construction) from δ1,…,δm\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{m}.

Lemma 3.4.

The LNDs Δ\Delta and δm\delta_{m} commute.

Proof.

We have

Δ∘δm=(∑i=1nfi​δi)∘δm=∑i=1nfi​δi∘δm=∑i=1nfi​δm∘δi=∑i=1nδm∘fi​δi=δm∘(∑i=1nfi​δi)=δm∘Δ.\Delta\circ\delta_{m}=\left(\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}\delta_{i}\right)\circ\delta_{m}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}\delta_{i}\circ\delta_{m}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}\delta_{m}\circ\delta_{i}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{m}\circ f_{i}\delta_{i}=\delta_{m}\circ\left(\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}\delta_{i}\right)=\delta_{m}\circ\Delta.

∎

Suppose m=2m=2. Starting with two commuting LNDs δ1\delta_{1} and δ2\delta_{2}, by C-construction, we obtain two commuting LNDs δ2\delta_{2} and δ3=Δ\delta_{3}=\Delta. Then we can start with these two commuting LNDs and again obtain by C-construction two commuting LNDs δ3\delta_{3} and δ4\delta_{4}. Iterating this procedure, we obtain a chain δ1,δ2,δ3,…\delta_{1},\delta_{2},\delta_{3},\ldots , where for each i⩾2i\geqslant 2, the derivation δi\delta_{i} commutes with both δi−1\delta_{i-1} and δi+1\delta_{i+1}. We call this chain a C-chain. A C-chain is called irreducible if all the LNDs δi\delta_{i} are irreducible.

3.1 Two variables

Let B=k⁡[x,y]B=k[x,y] and δ1,δ2\delta_{1},\delta_{2} be two commuting non-equivalent LNDs. Then C-construction gives δ3=λ​δ1+σ​δ2\delta_{3}=\lambda\delta_{1}+\sigma\delta_{2}, where σ∈Ker​δ2\sigma\in{\rm Ker}~\delta_{2}, λ∈k\lambda\in k and δ3\delta_{3} commutes with δ2\delta_{2}. It turns out that in case when δ2\delta_{2} is irreducible, each LND commuting with δ2\delta_{2} can be obtained by C-construction from δ1\delta_{1} and δ2\delta_{2}.

Lemma 3.5.

Suppose DD and EE are commuting non-equivalent LNDs of BB. Assume DD is irreducible. Let E′E^{\prime} be an LND of BB commuting with DD. Then E′=λ​E+σ​DE^{\prime}=\lambda E+\sigma D, where σ∈Ker​D\sigma\in{\rm Ker}~D and λ∈k∗\lambda\in k^{*}.

Proof.

By Theorem 2.7, there exist f,g∈k⁡[x,y]f,g\in k[x,y] such that k⁡[x,y]=k⁡[f,g]k[x,y]=k[f,g] and D=∂∂fD=\frac{\partial}{\partial f}. Let us consider restrictions ε\varepsilon and ε′\varepsilon^{\prime} of EE and E′E^{\prime} respectively to Ker​D=k⁡[g]{\rm Ker}~D=k[g]. Since D​E=E​DDE=ED and D​E′=E′​DDE^{\prime}=E^{\prime}D, both ε\varepsilon, ε′∈LND⁡(k⁡[g])\varepsilon^{\prime}\in{\rm LND}(k[g]). So we have ε=μ​∂∂g\varepsilon=\mu\frac{\partial}{\partial g}, ε′=μ′​∂∂g\varepsilon^{\prime}=\mu^{\prime}\frac{\partial}{\partial g}, where μ,μ′∈k\mu,\mu^{\prime}\in k. If μ=0\mu=0, then E|Ker​D=0E|_{{\rm Ker}~D}=0 and consequently EE and DD are equivalent, which is a contradiction. So μ≠0\mu\neq 0. Let λ=μ′μ\lambda=\frac{\mu^{\prime}}{\mu} and F=E′−λ​EF=E^{\prime}-\lambda E. Then F​D=D​FFD=DF and F⁡(g)=0F(g)=0. Since F⁡(g)=0F(g)=0, we have F=σ​∂∂fF=\sigma\frac{\partial}{\partial f} for some σ∈B\sigma\in B. We have ∂σ∂f=D⁡(σ)=D​F​(f)=F​D​(f)=F⁡(1)=0\frac{\partial\sigma}{\partial f}=D(\sigma)=DF(f)=FD(f)=F(1)=0. So, E′=σ​D+λ​EE^{\prime}=\sigma D+\lambda E, where σ=σ⁡(g)∈Ker​D\sigma=\sigma(g)\in{\rm Ker}~D and λ∈k∗\lambda\in k^{*}. ∎

Corollary 3.6.

Let RR be an affine kk-domain with field of fractions KK. Suppose DD and EE are commuting non-equivalent RR-LNDs of R⁡[x,y]R[x,y]. Assume DD is irreducible. Let E′E^{\prime} be an RR-LND of R⁡[x,y]R[x,y] commuting with DD. Then there exist non-zero elements s,r∈Rs,r\in R and q∈Ker​Dq\in{\rm Ker}~D such that s​E′=r​E+q​D.sE^{\prime}=rE+qD.

Proof.

The LNDs DD, EE, and E′E^{\prime} induce LNDs of K⁡[x,y]K[x,y]. By Lemma 3.5, E′=λ​E+σ​DE^{\prime}=\lambda E+\sigma D, where λ∈K∗\lambda\in K^{*}, σ∈K⁡[x,y]\sigma\in K[x,y] and σ∈Ker​D\sigma\in{\rm Ker}~D. There exist non-zero elements s,r∈Rs,r\in R such that r=s​λ∈Rr=s\lambda\in R and q=s​σ∈R⁡[x,y]q=s\sigma\in R[x,y]. Then s​E′=r​E+q​DsE^{\prime}=rE+qD. ∎

Let δ∈LND⁡(k⁡[x,y])\delta\in{\rm LND}(k[x,y]) be irreducible. By Theorem 2.7, there exist f,g∈k⁡[x,y]f,g\in k[x,y] such that k⁡[x,y]=k⁡[f,g]k[x,y]=k[f,g] and δ=∂∂g\delta=\frac{\partial}{\partial g}. Let α\alpha be the automorphism of k⁡[x,y]k[x,y] given by (x,y)↦(f,g)(x,y)\mapsto(f,g). Let us denote by Ψ⁡(δ)\Psi(\delta) the right coset T2​(k)​αT_{2}(k)\alpha. The association class of an LND δ\delta, denoted by [δ][\delta], is defined to be {ζ∈LND(B)|ζ=λδ,λ∈k∗}\{\zeta\in{\rm LND}(B)~|~\zeta=\lambda\delta,\lambda\in k^{*}\}.

Lemma 3.7.

The mapping Ψ\Psi gives a bijection between association classes of irreducible LNDs of k⁡[x,y]k[x,y] and right cosets of T2​(k)T_{2}(k).

Proof.

Let δ∈LND⁡(k⁡[x,y])\delta\in{\rm LND}(k[x,y]) be irreducible. Suppose α:(x,y)↦(f,g)\alpha:(x,y)\mapsto(f,g) and α1:(x,y)↦(f1,g1)\alpha_{1}\colon(x,y)\mapsto(f_{1},g_{1}) be two distinct automorphisms such that ∂∂g=δ=∂∂g1.\dfrac{\partial}{\partial g}=\delta=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial g_{1}}. Then Ker​δ=k⁡[f]=k⁡[f1]{\rm Ker}~\delta=k[f]=k[f_{1}]. Therefore, f1=a​f+bf_{1}=af+b, where a∈k∗a\in k^{*} and b∈kb\in k. Then, we have g1=c​g+P⁡(f)g_{1}=cg+P(f) where c∈k∗c\in k^{*} and P⁡(f)∈k⁡[f]P(f)\in k[f]. So, right cosets T2​(k)​α\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\alpha and T2​(k)​α1\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\alpha_{1} coincide. Now let us consider λ​δ\lambda\delta, λ∈k∗\lambda\in k^{*}. It corresponds to the automorphism α′:(x,y)↦(f,gλ)\alpha^{\prime}:(x,y)\mapsto(f,\frac{g}{\lambda}). Then Ψ⁡(δ)=T2​(k)​α=T2​(k)​α′=Ψ⁡(λ​δ)\Psi(\delta)=\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\alpha=\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\alpha^{\prime}=\Psi(\lambda\delta). Thus Ψ\Psi induces a well-defined map from the set of association classes of δ\delta to the set of right cosets of T2​(k){\rm T}_{2}(k). For convenience, we also call that map Ψ\Psi.

Suppose T2​(k)​α=T2​(k)​α1\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\alpha=\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\alpha_{1}. Then f1=a​f+bf_{1}=af+b and g1=c​g+P⁡(f)g_{1}=cg+P(f), where a,c∈k∗a,c\in k^{*}, b∈kb\in k and P⁡(f)∈k⁡[f]P(f)\in k[f]. Therefore, ∂∂g1=1c​∂∂g\frac{\partial}{\partial g_{1}}=\frac{1}{c}\frac{\partial}{\partial g}. This provides injectivity of Ψ\Psi. For each automorphism α:(x,y)↦(f,g)\alpha\colon(x,y)\mapsto(f,g) we have T2​(k)​α=Ψ⁡(∂∂g)\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\alpha=\Psi\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial g}\right). Therefore, Ψ\Psi is surjective. ∎

Lemma 3.8.

Let β∈Af2​(k)\beta\in{\rm Af}_{2}(k) and α∈Aut⁡(k[2])\alpha\in{\rm Aut}(k^{[2]}). Let D,E∈LND⁡(k[2])D,E\in{\rm LND}(k^{[2]}) be such that for the association classes [D][D] and [E][E], we have Ψ⁡([D])=T2​(k)​α\Psi([D])=\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\alpha and Ψ⁡([E])=T2​(k)​β∘α\Psi([E])=\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\beta\circ\alpha. Then DD and EE commute.

Proof.

Denote α=(f,g)\alpha=(f,g). We can assume that D⁡(f)=0D(f)=0, D⁡(g)=1D(g)=1. Then

β∘α:(xy)↦(a11a12a21a22)​(fg)+(b1b2),\beta\circ\alpha\colon\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}\\ a_{21}&a_{22}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}f\\ g\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}b_{1}\\ b_{2}\end{pmatrix},

where (a11a12a21a22)∈GL2​(k)\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}\\ a_{21}&a_{22}\end{pmatrix}\in{\rm GL}_{2}(k) and b1,b2∈kb_{1},b_{2}\in k. We can further assume that

E⁡(a11​f+a12​g+b1)=a11​E​(f)+a12​E​(g)=0​ and ​E​(a21​f+a22​g+b2)=a21​E​(f)+a22​E​(g)=1.E(a_{11}f+a_{12}g+b_{1})=a_{11}E(f)+a_{12}E(g)=0\text{ and }E(a_{21}f+a_{22}g+b_{2})=a_{21}E(f)+a_{22}E(g)=1.

Therefore, E⁡(f),E⁡(g)∈kE(f),E(g)\in k. So, we have

Thus, E​D=D​EED=DE. ∎

Proposition 3.9.

Each irreducible δ∈LND⁡(k[2])\delta\in{\rm LND}(k^{[2]}) can be constructed from an irreducible C-chain starting from δ1=∂∂x\delta_{1}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x} and δ2=∂∂y\delta_{2}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}.

Proof.

Let α∈Ψ⁡(D)\alpha\in\Psi(D). By Theorem 2.2, we can decompose α=ξm∘…∘ξ1\alpha=\xi_{m}\circ\ldots\circ\xi_{1}, where each ξj∈Af2​(k)∪T2​(k)\xi_{j}\in{\rm Af}_{2}(k)\cup{\rm T}_{2}(k). Consider sequence of right cosets

T2​(k),T2​(k)​ξ1,T2​(k)​ξ2∘ξ1,…,T2​(k)​ξm∘…∘ξ1.\mathrm{T}_{2}(k),\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\xi_{1},\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\xi_{2}\circ\xi_{1},\ldots,\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\xi_{m}\circ\ldots\circ\xi_{1}.

For any ii, if T2​(k)​γi=T2​(k)​ξs∘…∘ξ1\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\gamma_{i}=\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\xi_{s}\circ\ldots\circ\xi_{1} and T2​(k)​γi+1=T2​(k)​ξs+1∘ξs∘…∘ξ1\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\gamma_{i+1}=\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\xi_{s+1}\circ\xi_{s}\circ\ldots\circ\xi_{1}, then ξs+1∈Af2​(k)∖T2​(k)\xi_{s+1}\in{\rm Af}_{2}(k)\setminus{\rm T}_{2}(k). By Lemma 3.8, δi\delta_{i} commutes with δi−1\delta_{i-1} and δi+1\delta_{i+1}. Hence, by Lemma 3.5, δi+1=σ​δi+λ​δi−1\delta_{i+1}=\sigma\delta_{i}+\lambda\delta_{i-1}, where σ∈Ker​δi\sigma\in{\rm Ker}~\delta_{i}, λ∈k∗\lambda\in k^{*}. Since α=ξm∘…∘ξ1\alpha=\xi_{m}\circ\ldots\circ\xi_{1}, we can put δl=δ\delta_{l}=\delta. Definition 3.10.

A C-chain, starting from ∂∂x\frac{\partial}{\partial x} and ∂∂y\frac{\partial}{\partial y} will be called a full C-chain.

The next result is a partial converse of Lemma 3.8

Lemma 3.11.

Suppose Δ\Delta and DD are commuting irreducible LNDs of k[2]k^{[2]}. Then there exist such α∈Ψ⁡(D)\alpha\in\Psi(D) and θ∈Af2​(k)\theta\in\mathrm{Af}_{2}(k) that θ∘α∈Ψ⁡(Δ)\theta\circ\alpha\in\Psi(\Delta).

Proof.

It is enough to consider the case when Δ\Delta and DD are non-equivalent. Indeed, if Δ=t​D\Delta=tD for some t∈k∗t\in k^{*}, then Ψ⁡(Δ)=Ψ⁡(D)\Psi(\Delta)=\Psi(D). Now suppose we have D=∂∂gD=\frac{\partial}{\partial g}, where τ:(x,y)↦(f,g)\tau\colon(x,y)\mapsto(f,g) is an automorphism from Ψ⁡(D)\Psi(D). Denote E=∂∂fE=\frac{\partial}{\partial f}. Then D​E=E​DDE=ED. By Lemma 3.5, Δ=σ​D+λ​E\Delta=\sigma D+\lambda E, where σ∈Ker​D=k⁡[f]\sigma\in{\rm Ker}~D=k[f] and λ∈k∗\lambda\in k^{*}. Let h∈k⁡[f]h\in k[f] be such that d​hd​f=σ\frac{dh}{df}=\sigma. We have Δ⁡(f)=λ\Delta(f)=\lambda, Δ⁡(g)=σ\Delta(g)=\sigma. Therefore Δ⁡(λ​g−h⁡(f))=0\Delta(\lambda g-h(f))=0. γ:(xy)↦(xλ​y−h⁡(x))\gamma\colon\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}x\\ \lambda y-h(x)\end{pmatrix}

Clearly, γ∈T2​(k).\gamma\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k). Then

α=γ∘τ:(xy)↦(fλ​g−h⁡(f)).\alpha=\gamma\circ\tau\colon\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}f\\ \lambda g-h(f)\end{pmatrix}.

Let us put

θ:(xy)↦(yx),θ∈Af2​(k).\theta\colon\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}y\\ x\end{pmatrix},\qquad\theta\in\mathrm{Af}_{2}(k).

We have α∈T2​(k)​τ=Ψ⁡(D)\alpha\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\tau=\Psi(D). Choose δ∈LND⁡(k⁡[x,y])\delta\in{\rm LND}(k[x,y]) such that Ψ⁡([δ])=T2​(k)​θ∘α\Psi([\delta])=\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\theta\circ\alpha. Then δ⁡(f)=μ\delta(f)=\mu, for some μ∈k∗\mu\in k^{*} and δ⁡(λ​g−h⁡(f))=0\delta(\lambda g-h(f))=0. Hence, δ⁡(g)=μ​σ​(f)λ\delta(g)=\frac{\mu\sigma(f)}{\lambda}. So, Δ=λμ​δ\Delta=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\delta, i.e. θ∘α∈Ψ⁡(Δ)\theta\circ\alpha\in\Psi(\Delta). ∎

We immediately have the following corollary.

Corollary 3.12.

Let δ1,δ2,…,δl\delta_{1},\delta_{2},\ldots,\delta_{l} be a full irreducible C-chain in k[2]k^{[2]}. Then there exists a chain of automorphisms α2=id,β2,…,αl\alpha_{2}=\mathrm{id},\beta_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{l} such that βi=τi∘αi\beta_{i}=\tau_{i}\circ\alpha_{i}, αi+1=γi∘βi\alpha_{i+1}=\gamma_{i}\circ\beta_{i}, where γi∈Af2​(k)\gamma_{i}\in\mathrm{Af}_{2}(k), τi∈T2​(k)\tau_{i}\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k), and αi,βi∈Ψ⁡(δi)\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\in\Psi(\delta_{i}), for each i∈{1,…,l}i\in\{1,\dots,l\}.

Proof.

We have α2=id∈Ψ⁡(∂∂y)=Ψ⁡(δ1)\alpha_{2}=\mathrm{id}\in\Psi(\frac{\partial}{\partial y})=\Psi(\delta_{1}). For each ii, by Lemma 3.11, there exist βi∈Ψ⁡(δi)\beta_{i}\in\Psi(\delta_{i}) and γi∈Af2​(k)\gamma_{i}\in\mathrm{Af}_{2}(k) such that αi+1:=γi∘βi∈Ψ⁡(δi+1)\alpha_{i+1}:=\gamma_{i}\circ\beta_{i}\in\Psi(\delta_{i+1}). Since αi,βi∈Ψ⁡(δi)=T2​(k)​αi\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\in\Psi(\delta_{i})=\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\alpha_{i}, we have βi=τi∘αi\beta_{i}=\tau_{i}\circ\alpha_{i}, where τi∈T2​(k)\tau_{i}\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k). ∎

Next we define the level of an LND.

Definition 3.13.

Let δ\delta be an irreducible LND of k⁡[x,y]k[x,y]. Assume δ1,δ2,…,δl=δ\delta_{1},\delta_{2},\ldots,\delta_{l}=\delta is a full irreducible C-chain with minimal possible ll. Let us define the level of δ\delta to be this integer ll and denote it by lev​(δ)(x,y)\mathrm{lev}(\delta)_{(x,y)}.

Remark 3.14.

The definition of level depends on the coordinate system chosen for k[2]k^{[2]}. Indeed, for an irreducible δ∈LND⁡(k[2])\delta\in{\rm LND}(k^{[2]}), there exist f,g∈k[2]f,g\in k^{[2]} such that k⁡[x,y]=k⁡[f,g]k[x,y]=k[f,g] and δ=∂∂f\delta=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial f}. Then lev​(δ)(f,g)=1\mathrm{lev}(\delta)_{(f,g)}=1. So for any irreducible LND of k[2]k^{[2]}, there exists a coordinate system of k[2]k^{[2]} with respect to which the level is one.

Remark 3.15.

Let φ∈Ψ⁡(δ)\varphi\in\Psi(\delta). Assume δ∉[∂∂x]∪[∂∂y]\delta\notin\Big[\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big]\cup\Big[\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\Big]. Then Corollary 3.12 implies that lev​(δ)(x,y)=m+2\mathrm{lev}(\delta)_{(x,y)}=m+2, where mm is the number of affine automorphisms in the shortest decomposition

φ=τm∘γm​…∘τ1∘γ1,\varphi=\tau_{m}\circ\gamma_{m}\ldots\circ\tau_{1}\circ\gamma_{1},

where each γi∈Af2​(k)\gamma_{i}\in{\rm Af}_{2}(k) and τi∈T2​(k)\tau_{i}\in{\rm T}_{2}(k) (1⩽i⩽m1\leqslant i\leqslant m). By Theorem 2.2, the condition that this decomposition is shortest is equivalent to saying that γi∉T2​(k)\gamma_{i}\notin\mathrm{T}_{2}(k), 1⩽i⩽m1\leqslant i\leqslant m and τj∉Af2​(k)\tau_{j}\notin\mathrm{Af}_{2}(k), 1⩽j⩽m−11\leqslant j\leqslant m-1. Note that, each γi\gamma_{i} can be decomposed as γi=τ′∘θ∘τ′′\gamma_{i}=\tau^{\prime}\circ\theta\circ\tau^{\prime\prime}, where τ′,τ′′∈T2​(k)\tau^{\prime},\tau^{\prime\prime}\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k) and θ\theta is the swapping

θ:(xy)↦(yx).\theta\colon\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}y\\ x\end{pmatrix}.

Therefore, we can say that lev​(δ)(x,y)=m+2\mathrm{lev}(\delta)_{(x,y)}=m+2, where mm is the number of swappings in the shortest decomposition φ=τm∘θ​…∘τ1∘θ∘τ0\varphi=\tau_{m}\circ\theta\ldots\circ\tau_{1}\circ\theta\circ\tau_{0}.

The next proposition shows that given an irreducible δ∈LND⁡(k[2])\delta\in{\rm LND}(k^{[2]}) with level ll with respect to a fixed coordinate system, the LNDs in a full irreducible minimal C-chain are unique up to multiplication by scalars.

Proposition 3.16.

Let δ\delta be an irreducible LND of k⁡[x,y]k[x,y] with lev​(δ)(x,y)=l\mathrm{lev}(\delta)_{(x,y)}=l. Assume

δ1,δ2,…,δl=δ​ and ​ρ1,ρ2,…,ρl=δ\delta_{1},\delta_{2},\ldots,\delta_{l}=\delta\ \text{ and }\ \rho_{1},\rho_{2},\ldots,\rho_{l}=\delta

are two full irreducible minimal C-chains with length ll . Then for each i∈{1,…,l}i\in\{1,\dots,l\}, we have ρi=λi​δi\rho_{i}=\lambda_{i}\delta_{i} for some non-zero λi∈k\lambda_{i}\in k.

Proof.

From two full irreducible minimal C-chains, by Corollary 3.12, we obtain two sequences of automorphisms: α1=id,β1,α2,β2,…,αl\alpha_{1}=\mathrm{id},\beta_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{l} and α1′=id,β1′,α2′,β2′,…,αl′\alpha^{\prime}_{1}=\mathrm{id},\beta^{\prime}_{1},\alpha^{\prime}_{2},\beta^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,\alpha^{\prime}_{l}. By construction, we have αl,αl′∈Ψ⁡(δ)\alpha_{l},\alpha^{\prime}_{l}\in\Psi(\delta). Hence, αl′∈T2​(k)​αl\alpha_{l}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\alpha_{l}. So there exists ω∈T2​(k)\omega\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k) such that αl′=ω∘αl\alpha^{\prime}_{l}=\omega\circ\alpha_{l}. Note that, βi=τi∘αi\beta_{i}=\tau_{i}\circ\alpha_{i} and αi+1=γi∘βi\alpha_{i+1}=\gamma_{i}\circ\beta_{i}, where γi∈Af2​(k)\gamma_{i}\in\mathrm{Af}_{2}(k), τi∈T2​(k)\tau_{i}\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k). Similarly, βi′=τi′∘αi′\beta^{\prime}_{i}=\tau^{\prime}_{i}\circ\alpha^{\prime}_{i}, αi+1′=γi′∘βi′\alpha^{\prime}_{i+1}=\gamma^{\prime}_{i}\circ\beta^{\prime}_{i}, where γi′∈Af2​(k)\gamma^{\prime}_{i}\in\mathrm{Af}_{2}(k), τi′∈T2​(k)\tau^{\prime}_{i}\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k). So, we obtain

γl−1′∘τl−1′∘…∘γ1′∘τ1′=αl′=ω∘αl=ω∘γl−1∘τl−1∘…∘γ1∘τ1.\gamma^{\prime}_{l-1}\circ\tau^{\prime}_{l-1}\circ\ldots\circ\gamma^{\prime}_{1}\circ\tau^{\prime}_{1}=\alpha^{\prime}_{l}=\omega\circ\alpha_{l}=\omega\circ\gamma_{l-1}\circ\tau_{l-1}\circ\ldots\circ\gamma_{1}\circ\tau_{1}.

Since ll is minimal, we have γi,γi′∉T2​(k)\gamma_{i},\gamma^{\prime}_{i}\notin\mathrm{T}_{2}(k) and τj,τj′∉Af2​(k)\tau_{j},\tau^{\prime}_{j}\notin\mathrm{Af}_{2}(k). By Theorem 2.2, we then have αj′=ηj∘αj\alpha^{\prime}_{j}=\eta_{j}\circ\alpha_{j} for each j∈{1,…,l}j\in\{1,\dots,l\}, where ηj∈T2​(k)∩Af2​(k)\eta_{j}\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k)\cap\mathrm{Af}_{2}(k). Therefore, Ψ−1​(αj)=Ψ−1​(αj′)\Psi^{-1}(\alpha_{j})=\Psi^{-1}(\alpha^{\prime}_{j}). Since αj∈Ψ⁡(δj)\alpha_{j}\in\Psi(\delta_{j}), αj′∈Ψ⁡(ρj)\alpha^{\prime}_{j}\in\Psi(\rho_{j}) and T2​(k)​αj=T2​(k)​αj′{\rm T}_{2}(k)\alpha_{j}={\rm T}_{2}(k)\alpha^{\prime}_{j}, by Lemma 3.7, we are done. ∎

3.2 LNDs of rank at most 22

This subsection shows that one can apply the C-construction to construct LNDs of k[n]k^{[n]} of rank at most 22. Let B=k⁡[x1,…,xn]B=k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] and D∈LND⁡(B)D\in{\rm LND}(B) such that rk​D⩽2{\rm rk}~D\leqslant 2. We can choose a system of variables such that k⁡[x3,…,xn]⊆Ker​Dk[x_{3},\ldots,x_{n}]\subseteq\mathrm{Ker}\,D. Then we can obtain DD from partial derivations by a construction similar to the C-construction.

Lemma 3.17.

Let RR be an affine kk-domain with field of fractions KK and DD an irreducible RR-LND of R⁡[x1,x2](=R[2])R[x_{1},x_{2}](=R^{[2]}). Then there exists a chain of irreducible LNDs of R⁡[x1,x2]R[x_{1},x_{2}]

∂1:=∂∂x1,∂2:=∂∂x2,∂3,…,∂l=D,\partial_{1}:=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}},\partial_{2}:=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}},\partial_{3},\dots,\partial_{l}=D,

such that for all ii, 1⩽i⩽l1\leqslant i\leqslant l, ∂i(R)=0\partial_{i}(R)=0 and

hi∂i=σ∂i−1+fi∂i−2h_{i}\partial_{i}=\sigma\partial_{i-1}+f_{i}\partial_{i-2}

for some σ∈Ker∂i−1\sigma\in{\rm Ker}~\partial_{i-1}, fi,hi∈R∖{0}f_{i},h_{i}\in R\setminus\{0\}.

Proof.

Since D⁡(R)=0D(R)=0, it induces an LND δ\delta of K⁡[x1,x2]K[x_{1},x_{2}]. Since DD is irreducible in R⁡[x1,x2]R[x_{1},x_{2}], so is δ\delta in K⁡[x1,x2]K[x_{1},x_{2}]. By Proposition 3.9, δ\delta can be constructed by a full irreducible C-chain {δi}i=1l\{\delta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{l} in K⁡[x1,x2]K[x_{1},x_{2}] starting from δ1=∂∂x1\delta_{1}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}} and δ2=∂∂x2\delta_{2}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}. For each ii, there exists gi∈K∗g_{i}\in K^{*} such that ∂i=giδi\partial_{i}=g_{i}\delta_{i} is an irreducible LND of R⁡[x1,x2]R[x_{1},x_{2}]. Note that ∂i−2\partial_{i-2} and ∂i\partial_{i} commutes with ∂i−1\partial_{i-1}. By Corollary 3.6, we have hi∂i=σ∂i−1+fi∂i−2h_{i}\partial_{i}=\sigma\partial_{i-1}+f_{i}\partial_{i-2} for some σ∈Ker∂i−1\sigma\in\mathrm{Ker}\,\partial_{i-1}, fi,hi∈R∖{0}f_{i},h_{i}\in R\setminus\{0\}. ∎

We immediately have the following corollary.

Corollary 3.18.

Let D∈LND⁡(k⁡[x1,…,xn])D\in{\rm LND}(k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]) be irreducible and D⁡(x3)=…=D⁡(xn)=0D(x_{3})=\ldots=D(x_{n})=0. Then there exists a chain of irreducible LNDs of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]

∂1:=∂∂x1,∂2:=∂∂x2,∂3,…,∂l=D,\partial_{1}:=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}},\partial_{2}:=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}},\partial_{3},\dots,\partial_{l}=D,

such that for all ii, 1⩽i⩽l1\leqslant i\leqslant l, we have ∂i(x3)=…=∂i(xn)=0\partial_{i}(x_{3})=\ldots=\partial_{i}(x_{n})=0 and

hi∂i=σ∂i−1+fi∂i−2h_{i}\partial_{i}=\sigma\partial_{i-1}+f_{i}\partial_{i-2}

for some σ∈Ker∂i−1\sigma\in\mathrm{Ker}\,\partial_{i-1}, fi,hi∈k⁡[x3,…,xn]∖{0}f_{i},h_{i}\in k[x_{3},\ldots,x_{n}]\setminus\{0\}.

Proof.

The proof follows from Lemma 3.17 by setting R=k⁡[x3,…,xn]R=k[x_{3},\dots,x_{n}]. ∎

We call this construction a Modified C-construction (denoted by MC-construction) and the chain ∂1,…,∂l\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{l} a full irreducible MC-chain. Like in the case of k[2]k^{[2]}, one can define the level of an irreducible LND DD of rank at most 22, as the length of the shortest full irreducible MC-chain ending at DD. As noted earlier, this level depends on the chosen coordinate system. We denote it by lev𝐱​(D)\mathrm{lev}_{\mathbf{x}}(D), where 𝐱={x1,x2,…,xn}\mathbf{x}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}\}. This motivates us to make the following definition. Suppose DD is an LND of k[n]k^{[n]} with rank at most 22. Let ΓD\Gamma_{D} denote the collection of all coordinate systems 𝐲={y1,…,yn}\mathbf{y}=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\} of k[n]k^{[n]} such that D⁡(yi)=0D(y_{i})=0 for i⩾3i\geqslant 3. We would like to define the universal level as minimal possible level among all such coordinate systems 𝐲\mathbf{y}.

Definition 3.19.

For an irreducible D∈LND⁡(k[n])D\in{\rm LND}(k^{[n]}) of rank at most 22, we define the universal level of DD, denoted by ulev⁡(D)\mathrm{ulev}(D) as

ulev⁡(D)=min𝐲∈ΓD⁡{lev𝐲​(D)|𝐲∈ΓD}.\mathrm{ulev}(D)=\min_{\mathbf{y}\in\Gamma_{D}}~\left\{\mathrm{lev}_{\mathbf{y}}(D)~|~\mathbf{y}\in\Gamma_{D}\right\}.

It easy to see that ulev⁡(D)\mathrm{ulev}(D) does not attain the value 22. Using universal level, one can characterize rank 11 LNDs and triangularizable LNDs of k[n]k^{[n]}.

Theorem 3.20.

Let D∈LND⁡(k[n])D\in{\rm LND}(k^{[n]}) be irreducible of r​a​n​krank at most 22. Then the following statements hold:

  1. (i)

    ulev⁡(D)=1⇔r​k​D=1\mathrm{ulev}(D)=1\Leftrightarrow rk\,D=1;

  2. (ii)

    ulev⁡(D)=3⇔D​is triangularizable LND of rank 2.\mathrm{ulev}(D)=3\Leftrightarrow D~\text{is triangularizable LND of rank 2}.

Proof.

(i) Suppose ulev⁡(D)=1\mathrm{ulev}(D)=1. Then there exists a coordinate system {y1,…,yn}\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\} of k[n]k^{[n]} such that D=∂∂y1D=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_{1}}. Hence, rk​D=1\mathrm{rk}\,D=1. Conversely, since DD is irreducible of rank 11, there exists a coordinate system of k[n]k^{[n]} in which DD is a partial derivation. Hence, ulev⁡(D)=1\mathrm{ulev}(D)=1.

(ii) The condition ulev⁡(D)=3\mathrm{ulev}(D)=3 is equivalent to the fact that there exists a coordinate system {y1,…,yn}\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\} of k[n]k^{[n]} such that

h⁡(y3,…,yn)​D=f⁡(y3,…,yn)​∂∂y1+σ⁡(y1,y3,y4,…,yn)​∂∂y2,h(y_{3},\ldots,y_{n})D=f(y_{3},\ldots,y_{n})\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_{1}}+\sigma(y_{1},y_{3},y_{4},\ldots,y_{n})\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_{2}},

for some f∈k⁡[y3,…,yn]f\in k[y_{3},\ldots,y_{n}] and σ∈Ker​∂∂x2=k⁡[y1,y3,…,yn]\sigma\in{\rm Ker}~\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}=k[y_{1},y_{3},\ldots,y_{n}]. Swapping y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} we obtain

h⁡(y3,…,yn)​D=f⁡(y3,…,yn)​∂∂y2+σ⁡(y2,y3,y4,…,yn)​∂∂y1.h(y_{3},\ldots,y_{n})D=f(y_{3},\ldots,y_{n})\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_{2}}+\sigma(y_{2},y_{3},y_{4},\ldots,y_{n})\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y_{1}}.

So, D⁡(y1)=σ⁡(y2,…,yn)h⁡(y3,…,yn)D(y_{1})=\dfrac{\sigma(y_{2},\ldots,y_{n})}{h(y_{3},\ldots,y_{n})} and D⁡(y2)=f⁡(y3,…,yn)h⁡(y3,…,yn)D(y_{2})=\dfrac{f(y_{3},\ldots,y_{n})}{h(y_{3},\ldots,y_{n})}. Since D⁡(y1),D⁡(y2)∈k[n]D(y_{1}),D(y_{2})\in k^{[n]}, it follows that D⁡(y1)∈k⁡[y2,…,yn]D(y_{1})\in k[y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}] and D⁡(y2)∈k⁡[y3,…,yn]D(y_{2})\in k[y_{3},\ldots,y_{n}]. Clearly, D⁡(y3)=…=D⁡(yn)=0D(y_{3})=\ldots=D(y_{n})=0. This implies triangularizability of DD and since ulev⁡(D)≠1{\rm ulev}(D)\neq 1, we must have rk​D=2{\rm rk}~D=2 by part (i).

Conversely, if DD is triangularizable of rank 22, then in some coordinate system {y1,…,yn}\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\}, we have

D⁡(y3)=…=D⁡(yn)=0,D⁡(y2)=f⁡(y3,…,yn),D⁡(y1)=h⁡(y2,…,yn),D(y_{3})=\ldots=D(y_{n})=0,\qquad D(y_{2})=f(y_{3},\ldots,y_{n}),\qquad D(y_{1})=h(y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}),

for suitable non-zero ff and hh. Then

D=h⁡(y2,…,yn)​∂∂y1+f⁡(y3,…,yn)​∂∂y2.D=h(y_{2},\ldots,y_{n})\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{1}}+f(y_{3},\ldots,y_{n})\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{2}}.

So ∂∂y2,∂∂y1,D\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{2}},\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{1}},D is an irreducible MC-chain. Hence ulev⁡(D)⩽3\mathrm{ulev}(D)\leqslant 3. But by (i), ulev⁡(D)≠1\mathrm{ulev}(D)\neq 1. Since universal level never equals 2, we have ulev⁡(D)=3\mathrm{ulev}(D)=3. ∎

Remark 3.21.

Since there are irreducible LNDs on k[3]k^{[3]} with universal level 11 or 33, it is natural to ask whether for an irreducible D∈LND⁡(k[3])D\in{\rm LND}(k^{[3]}), can ulev⁡(D)>3​?{\rm ulev}(D)>3? In Section 4, we give an example of an LND on k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z] with universal level 44 (see Example 4.14). But we don’t have any example of an LND for which we can prove that the universal level is 55 or more. So we end this section with the following question.

Question 3.22.

For an irreducible D∈LND⁡(k[n])D\in{\rm LND}(k^{[n]}), n⩾3n\geqslant 3, can ulev⁡(D)>4{\rm ulev}(D)>4?

We have an explicit candidate of an LND DD of k[3]k^{[3]} with ulev⁡(D)=5\mathrm{ulev}(D)=5, see Remark 4.16 and Question 4.17. If we are given an LND DD of k⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]k[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}] with D⁡(x3)=…=D⁡(xn)=0D(x_{3})=\ldots=D(x_{n})=0, we can consider its extension δ\delta to k⁡(x3,…,xn)​[x1,x2]k(x_{3},\ldots,x_{n})[x_{1},x_{2}] and take α∈Ψ⁡(δ)\alpha\in\Psi(\delta). This automorphism α\alpha can be algorithmically decomposed onto a composition of triangular and affine ones. This gives us an algorithm for computing lev(x1,…,xn)​D\mathrm{lev}_{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})}D. This leads to the following question.

Question 3.23.

Is there an algorithm to compute the universal level of a given irreducible LND of k[n]k^{[n]} of rank at most 22, where n⩾3n\geqslant 3?

4 Rank 𝟐\mathbf{2} derivations

In this section, we study locally nilpotent derivations of B=k[3]B=k^{[3]}. We first give a necessary and sufficient condition for a locally nilpotent derivation to have a non-equivalent commuting locally nilpotent derivation.

Proposition 4.1.

Let B=k[3]B=k^{[3]} and D(≠0)∈LND⁡(B)D(\neq 0)\in{\rm LND}(B). Then there exists E(≠0)∈LND⁡(B)E(\neq 0)\in{\rm LND}(B) such that D​E=E​DDE=ED and Ker​D≠Ker​E{\rm Ker}~D\neq{\rm Ker}~E if and only if there exists g∈Bg\in B such that D⁡(g)=f⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]D(g)=f(x)\in k[x] and xx is a variable of Ker​D{\rm Ker}~D.

Proof.

Suppose D​E=E​DDE=ED and Ker​D≠Ker​E{\rm Ker}~D\neq{\rm Ker}~E. Then, by Proposition 2.14, there exists a variable xx of BB such that Ker​D∩Ker​E=k⁡[x]{\rm Ker}~D\cap{\rm Ker}~E=k[x]. By Lemma 2.15(i), xx is a variable of Ker​D{\rm Ker}~D. Since D​E=E​DDE=ED and Ker​D≠Ker​E{\rm Ker}~D\neq{\rm Ker}~E, DD restricts to δ(≠0)∈LND⁡(Ker​E)\delta(\neq 0)\in{\rm LND}({\rm Ker}~E). Since δ\delta is non-zero, it has a local slice gg. Then D⁡(g)=δ⁡(g)∈Ker​δ=k⁡[x]D(g)=\delta(g)\in{\rm Ker}~\delta=k[x].

Conversely, suppose that there exists g∈Bg\in B such that D⁡(g)=f⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]D(g)=f(x)\in k[x] and xx is a variable in Ker​D{\rm Ker}~D. Then, by Lemma 2.15(ii), xx is a variable in BB such that D⁡(x)=0D(x)=0. Let B=k⁡[x,y,z]B=k[x,y,z] and consider the derivation

E:=Jac(x,g,⋅)=∂g∂y∂∂z−∂g∂z∂∂y.E:={\rm Jac}(x,g,\cdot)=\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}-\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial z}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}.

Let Ker​D=k⁡[x,p]{\rm Ker}~D=k[x,p] for some p∈Bp\in B. By Theorem 2.18, we have

D=hJac(x,p,.)=h(∂p∂y∂∂z−∂p∂z∂∂y),whereh∈k[x,p]∖{0}.D=h~{\rm Jac}(x,p,.)=h\left(\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial y}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}-\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial z}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\right),~\text{where}~h\in k[x,p]\setminus\{0\}.

Since D⁡(g)=f⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]D(g)=f(x)\in k[x], we have h|f⁡(x)h\mid f(x). So we also have h=h⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]h=h(x)\in k[x]. Note that

h⁡(x)​E​(p)=h⁡(x)​(∂g∂y​∂p∂z−∂g∂z​∂p∂y)=−D⁡(g)=−f⁡(x).h(x)E(p)=h(x)\left(\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y}\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial z}-\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial z}\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial y}\right)=-D(g)=-f(x).

Hence E2​(p)=0E^{2}(p)=0. Since gg is a local slice of DD, we have k⁡[x,y,z,1f⁡(x)]=k⁡[x,p,1f⁡(x)]​[g]k[x,y,z,\frac{1}{f(x)}]=k[x,p,\frac{1}{f(x)}][g]. So any element s∈Bs\in B can be represented as

s=fs​(x,p,g)fms,where​fs∈k⁡[x,p,g]​and​ms∈ℕ∪{0}.s=\dfrac{f_{s}(x,p,g)}{f^{m_{s}}},~\text{where}~f_{s}\in k[x,p,g]~\text{and}~m_{s}\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}.

Since E⁡(x)=E⁡(g)=E2​(p)=0E(x)=E(g)=E^{2}(p)=0, we obtain E∈LND⁡(B)E\in{\rm LND}(B). Now we have

E​D​(x)=D​E​(x)=0,E​D​(g)=E⁡(f⁡(x))=0=D​E​(g),ED(x)=DE(x)=0,\qquad ED(g)=E(f(x))=0=DE(g),
h⁡(x)​D​E​(p)=D⁡(h⁡(x)​E​(p))=D⁡(−f⁡(x))=0=h⁡(x)​E​D​(p).h(x)DE(p)=D(h(x)E(p))=D(-f(x))=0=h(x)ED(p).

Since DD and EE commute on k⁡[x,p,g]k[x,p,g] and D⁡(x)=E⁡(x)=0D(x)=E(x)=0, they also commute on BB because of B⁡[1f⁡(x)]=k⁡[x,p,g,1f⁡(x)].B[\frac{1}{f(x)}]=k[x,p,g,\frac{1}{f(x)}]. ∎

Remark 4.2.

The above proof is similar to the proof given in [6, Lemma 4.1]. The authors prove the existence of a locally nilpotent derivation commuting with DD, under the hypothesis that DD is irreducible of r​a​n​k​2rank~2. The condition that “there exists g∈Bg\in B such that D⁡(g)=f⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]D(g)=f(x)\in k[x] and xx is a variable in Ker​D{\rm Ker}\,D” is automatically satisfied if gg is a minimal local slice of DD [6, Lemma 2.5, Theorem 3.1] under the assumption that rk​D≠1\rm{rk}~D\neq 1. Our result holds true for any locally nilpotent derivation of BB of rank\rm{rank} at most 22 without any assumption on irreducibility.

We next claim an elementary lemma.

Lemma 4.3.

Let B=k[3]B=k^{[3]} and D∈LND⁡(B)D\in{\rm LND}(B) be irreducible of rank at most 2. Then there exists a variable xx of BB and g∈Bg\in B such that D⁡(g)=f⁡(x)∈Ker​DD(g)=f(x)\in{\rm Ker}~D.

Proof.

Since rk​D⩽2\mathrm{rk}\,D\leqslant 2, there exists a variable xx of BB such that x∈Ker​Dx\in{\rm Ker}~D. Then DD extends to an irreducible locally nilpotent derivation D~\tilde{D} on k​(x)​[y,z]k(x)[y,z]. By Theorem 2.7, D~\tilde{D} has a slice, i.e., there exist g∈Bg\in B and f∈k⁡[x]∖{0}f\in k[x]\setminus\{0\} such that D~​(gf)=1\tilde{D}(\frac{g}{f})=1. Hence D⁡(g)=f⁡(x)D(g)=f(x). ∎

We immediately have the following corollary.

Corollary 4.4.

Let B=k[3]B=k^{[3]}, D∈LND⁡(B)D\in{\rm LND}(B) be of rank 2 and A:=Ker​DA:={\rm Ker}~D. Let x∈Ax\in A and x′∈Ax^{\prime}\in A be any other variable of BB, then there exist λ∈k∗\lambda\in k^{*} and μ∈k\mu\in k such that x′=λ​x+μx^{\prime}=\lambda x+\mu.

Proof.

Without loss of generality we may assume DD to be irreducible. By Lemma 4.3, there exist g,g′∈Bg,g^{\prime}\in B such that D⁡(g)=f⁡(x)D(g)=f(x) and D⁡(g′)=h⁡(x′)D(g^{\prime})=h(x^{\prime}) for some f∈k⁡[x]∖{0}f\in k[x]\setminus\{0\} and h∈k⁡[x′]∖{0}h\in k[x^{\prime}]\setminus\{0\}. By Theorem 2.10 (ii), there exists v∈Av\in A such that A∩D​B=(v)A\cap DB=(v). Then v|fv\mid f and v|hv\mid h. So there exists a⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]a(x)\in k[x] and b⁡(x′)∈k⁡[x′]b(x^{\prime})\in k[x^{\prime}] such that v=a⁡(x)=b⁡(x′)v=a(x)=b(x^{\prime}). Since rk​D≠1\rm{rk}~D\neq 1, v∉kv\notin k. So xx and x′x^{\prime} are algebraically dependent over kk. Since k⁡[x]k[x] is algebraically closed in BB, we have x′∈k⁡[x]x^{\prime}\in k[x]. But x′x^{\prime} is a variable of BB and hence has to be a linear polynomial in xx. Thus there exist λ∈k∗\lambda\in k^{*} and μ∈k\mu\in k such that x′=λ​x+μx^{\prime}=\lambda x+\mu. ∎

Let us now describe all LNDs of BB commuting with a fixed non-zero irreducible LND DD.

Theorem 4.5.

Let D∈LND⁡(B)D\in{\rm LND}(B) be irreducible. Then the following statements hold:

  1. (i)

    if rk​D=3\mathrm{rk}\,D=3, then all LNDs commuting with DD are equivalent to DD;

  2. (ii)

    if rk​D=2\mathrm{rk}\,D=2, fix such a variable xx of BB that x∈A=Ker​Dx\in A=\mathrm{Ker}\,D. Then there exists E∈LND⁡(B)E\in{\rm LND}(B), non-equivalent to DD such that D​E=E​DDE=ED and for any E′∈LND⁡(B)E^{\prime}\in{\rm LND}(B) be such that D​E′=E′​DDE^{\prime}=E^{\prime}D, there exist α1,α2∈k⁡[x]∖{0}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in k[x]\setminus\{0\} and β∈Ker​D\beta\in{\rm Ker}~D such that

    α1​E′=α2​E+β​D.\alpha_{1}E^{\prime}=\alpha_{2}E+\beta D.

    Moreover Ker​D∩Ker​E=Ker​D∩Ker​E′=k⁡[x]{\rm Ker}\,D\cap{\rm Ker}\,E={\rm Ker}\,D\cap{\rm Ker}\,E^{\prime}=k[x];

  3. (iii)

    if rk​D=1\mathrm{rk}\,D=1, then for each variable xx of AA there exists E∈LND⁡(B)E\in{\rm LND}(B) non-equivalent to DD such that D​E=E​DDE=ED, Ker​D∩Ker​E=k⁡[x]{\rm Ker}\,D\cap{\rm Ker}\,E=k[x] and there exists a systen of coordinates {x,y,z}\{x,y,z\} in BB such that EE is triangular with respect to this system. If E′∈LND⁡(B)E^{\prime}\in{\rm LND}(B) be such that D​E′=E′​DDE^{\prime}=E^{\prime}D and Ker​D∩Ker​E′=k⁡[x]{\rm Ker}\,D\cap{\rm Ker}\,E^{\prime}=k[x], then E′E^{\prime} is triangular with respect to {x,y,z}\{x,y,z\} and there exist α1,α2,∈k⁡[x]∖{0}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\in k[x]\setminus\{0\} and β∈Ker​D\beta\in{\rm Ker}~D such that

    α1​E′=α2​E+β​D.\alpha_{1}E^{\prime}=\alpha_{2}E+\beta D.
Proof.

Since DD is irreducible, if there is a non-equivalent EE such that D​E=E​DDE=ED, then by Proposition 4.1, we can choose g∈Bg\in B such that D⁡(g)∈k⁡[x]D(g)\in k[x], where xx is a variable of BB contained in Ker​D{\rm Ker}~D. This proves (i).

If rk​D=2{\rm rk}~D=2, then such an EE exists by Lemma 4.3 and Proposition 4.1. By Proposition 2.14, Ker​D∩Ker​E=k⁡[f]\mathrm{Ker}\,D\cap\mathrm{Ker}\,E=k[f], where ff is a variable of BB. By Corollary 4.4, k⁡[f]=k⁡[x]k[f]=k[x]. We can say the same about E′E^{\prime}. Therefore, D,ED,E and E′E^{\prime} are k⁡[x]k[x]-LNDs of BB. So, we can apply Corollary 3.6, which proves (ii).

If rk​D=1\mathrm{rk}\,D=1, then there a coordinate system (x,y,z)(x,y,z) of BB such that D=∂∂zD=\frac{\partial}{\partial z} and A=k⁡[x,y]A=k[x,y]. Clearly, such an EE exists by Lemma 4.3 and Proposition 4.1. As E​D=D​EED=DE, EE restricts to an LND on AA. Since E⁡(x)=0E(x)=0, by Proposition 2.16, E⁡(y)∈k⁡[x]E(y)\in k[x]. Again by Proposition 2.16, E⁡(z)∈A=k⁡[x,y]E(z)\in A=k[x,y]. So EE is triangular with respect to the coordinate system (x,y,z)(x,y,z). Similar argument shows that E′E^{\prime} is also triangular and the rest of the proof follows from Corollary 3.6.

∎

Let us now apply the theory of Section 3 to investigate LNDs of rank 22 of B=k[3]B=k^{[3]}.

Proposition 4.6.

Let DD be an irreducible LND of B=k[3]B=k^{[3]} of rank at most 22. Suppose B=k⁡[x,y,z]B=k[x,y,z] and x∈A=Ker​Dx\in A=\mathrm{Ker}\,D. Let 𝐱={x,y,z}\mathbf{x}=\{x,y,z\} and let Γ\Gamma denote the collection of all coordinate systems 𝐱′={x,y′,z′}\mathbf{x^{\prime}}=\{x,y^{\prime},z^{\prime}\}, where y′,z′∈By^{\prime},z^{\prime}\in B. Then

ulev⁡(D)=min𝐱′∈Γ⁡{lev𝐱′​(D)|𝐱′∈Γ}.\mathrm{ulev}(D)=\min_{\mathbf{x^{\prime}}\in\Gamma}~\left\{\mathrm{lev}_{\mathbf{x^{\prime}}}(D)~|~\mathbf{x^{\prime}}\in\Gamma\right\}.
Proof.

Let xx be a variable of BB contained in AA. By Corollary 3.18, DD can be obtained by a full MC-chain ∂∂x,∂∂y,…,D\frac{\partial}{\partial x},\frac{\partial}{\partial y},\ldots,D. By definition, universal level of DD is the minimal level of D with respect to a coordinate system {x′,y′,z′}\{x^{\prime},y^{\prime},z^{\prime}\} with x′∈Ax^{\prime}\in A. If rk​D=2\mathrm{rk}\,D=2, Corollary 4.4 implies x′=λ​x+μx^{\prime}=\lambda x+\mu. So, {x,y′,z′}\{x,y^{\prime},z^{\prime}\} is also a system of coordinates and since k⁡(x′)=k⁡(x)k(x^{\prime})=k(x), lev(x′,y′,z′)​(D)=lev(x,y′,z′)​(D)\mathrm{lev}_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime},z^{\prime})}(D)=\mathrm{lev}_{(x,y^{\prime},z^{\prime})}(D). So, to compute ulev⁡(D)\mathrm{ulev}\,(D) we need to take minimal lev(x,y′,z′)​(D)\mathrm{lev}_{(x,y^{\prime},z^{\prime})}(D). If rk​D=1\mathrm{rk}~D=1 and DD is irreducible, then by Proposition 2.12, DD has a slice, say ss. By Theorem 2.18, A=k⁡[x,f]A=k[x,f], for some f∈Bf\in B. Then, by Theorem 2.5, B=k⁡[x,f,s]B=k[x,f,s] and D=∂∂sD=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial s}. Therefore, lev(x,f,s)​(D)=1\mathrm{lev}_{(x,f,s)}(D)=1. So, in this case too, ulev⁡(D)=min𝐱′∈Π⁡{lev𝐱′​(D)|𝐱′∈Γ}\mathrm{ulev}(D)=\min_{\mathbf{x^{\prime}}\in\Pi}~\left\{\mathrm{lev}_{\mathbf{x^{\prime}}}(D)~|~\mathbf{x^{\prime}}\in\Gamma\right\}. ∎

As before, let D∈LND⁡(B)D\in{\rm LND}(B) be irreducible of rank at most 22. Let us also fix a coordinate system {x,y,z}\{x,y,z\} of BB such that D⁡(x)=0D(x)=0. Let α\alpha be a k⁡(x)k(x)-automorphism of k​(x)​[y,z]k(x)[y,z]. By θ\theta, we denote the swapping

(yz)↦(zy)\begin{pmatrix}y\\ z\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}z\\ y\end{pmatrix}
Definition 4.7.

Let us define the complexity of α\alpha, denoted by c⁡(α)c(\alpha) to be the minimal number mm such that there exist τ0,τ1​…,τm∈T2​(k⁡(x))\tau_{0},\tau_{1}\ldots,\tau_{m}\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k(x)) with the property that

τm∘θ∘τm−1∘…∘θ∘τ0∘α∈Aut⁡(k⁡[x,y,z]).\tau_{m}\circ\theta\circ\tau_{m-1}\circ\ldots\circ\theta\circ\tau_{0}\circ\alpha\in\mathrm{Aut}(k[x,y,z]).
Remark 4.8.

The number mm in the previous definition exists. Indeed, it follows from Remark 3.15 that there exists η0,η1​…,ηN∈T2​(k⁡(x))\eta_{0},\eta_{1}\ldots,\eta_{N}\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k(x)) that

ηN∘θ∘ηN−1∘…∘θ∘η0∘α=id.\eta_{N}\circ\theta\circ\eta_{N-1}\circ\ldots\circ\theta\circ\eta_{0}\circ\alpha=\mathrm{id}.

Let us consider the extension of DD as an LND of k​(x)​[y,z]k(x)[y,z], which we also denote by DD and take Ψ⁡(D)\Psi(D) as in Section 3.1.

Theorem 4.9.

Suppose DD is an irreducible LND of rank 2. Then

ulev⁡(D)=c⁡(α)+2,where​α∈Ψ⁡(D).{\rm ulev}(D)=c(\alpha)+2,~~\text{where}~~\alpha\in\Psi(D).
Proof.

Let us recall that α∈Ψ⁡(D)\alpha\in\Psi(D) takes yy to a generator of Ker​D\mathrm{Ker}\,D and zz to a slice of DD. Since the mapping Ψ\Psi depends on the coordinate system, let us write α∈Ψ(x,y,z)​(D)\alpha\in\Psi_{(x,y,z)}(D). If we take another coordinate system {x,y′,z′}\{x,y^{\prime},z^{\prime}\}, then we can consider the automorphism φ\varphi of BB given by (x,y′,z′)↦(x,y,z)(x,y^{\prime},z^{\prime})\mapsto(x,y,z). In this system of variables we also can consider Ψ(x,y′,z′)​(D)\Psi_{(x,y^{\prime},z^{\prime})}(D). It is easy to see that α∘φ∈Ψ(x,y′,z′)​(D)\alpha\circ\varphi\in\Psi_{(x,y^{\prime},z^{\prime})}(D). Let us also recall that lev(x,y,z)​(D)=m+2\mathrm{lev}_{(x,y,z)}(D)=m+2, where mm is the number of affine automorphisms in the decomposition of α=τm∘γm​…∘τ1∘γ1\alpha=\tau_{m}\circ\gamma_{m}\ldots\circ\tau_{1}\circ\gamma_{1}, τi∈T2​(k⁡(x))\tau_{i}\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k(x)), γi∈Af2​(k⁡(x))\gamma_{i}\in\mathrm{Af}_{2}(k(x)) (1⩽i⩽m1\leqslant i\leqslant m), see Remark 3.15. Equivalently, lev(x,y,z)​(D)=m+2\mathrm{lev}_{(x,y,z)}(D)=m+2, where mm is the number of swappings θ\theta in the decomposition α=τm∘θ​…∘τ1∘θ∘τ0\alpha=\tau_{m}\circ\theta\ldots\circ\tau_{1}\circ\theta\circ\tau_{0}, τj∈T2​(k⁡(x))\tau_{j}\in\mathrm{T}_{2}(k(x)) (0⩽j⩽m0\leqslant j\leqslant m). By Proposition 4.6, ulev⁡(D){\rm ulev}(D) is the minimal lev(x,y′,z′)​(D)\mathrm{lev}_{(x,y^{\prime},z^{\prime})}(D), where k⁡[x,y,z]=k⁡[x,y′,z′]k[x,y,z]=k[x,y^{\prime},z^{\prime}]. It follows from the definition, that c⁡(α)=c⁡(α∘φ)c(\alpha)=c(\alpha\circ\varphi) for any φ∈Aut⁡(B)\varphi\in{\rm Aut}(B). Thus if we take mm to be the minimal number of swappings θ\theta in the decomposition of α∘φ\alpha\circ\varphi for all φ∈Aut⁡(B)\varphi\in\mathrm{Aut}(B), such that φ⁡(x)=x\varphi(x)=x, then ulev⁡(D)=m+2{\rm ulev}(D)=m+2. The result follows. ∎

Remark 4.10.

If rk​D=1\mathrm{rk}\,D=1, then ulev​D=1\mathrm{ulev}\,D=1 and the complexity of α\alpha equals zero.

The following corollary gives a criterion for an irreducible LND of rank at most 22 to be triangularizable.

Corollary 4.11.

Let DD be an irreducible LND of k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z] such that D⁡(x)=0D(x)=0. Consider α∈Ψ⁡(D)\alpha\in\Psi(D). Then

D​ is triangularizable⇔c⁡(α)⩽1.D~\text{ is triangularizable}~\Leftrightarrow~c(\alpha)\leqslant 1.

Moreover, if DD is triangularizable, then there exist u1,v0∈k⁡(x)u_{1},v_{0}\in k(x), f,g∈k⁡[x,y,z]f,g\in k[x,y,z], F0∈k​(x)[1]F_{0}\in k(x)^{[1]} and ζ∈Autk⁡[x]​(k⁡[x,y,z])\zeta\in{\rm Aut}_{k[x]}(k[x,y,z]) such that

ζ⁡(y)=u1​(v0​g+F0​(f)).\zeta(y)=u_{1}(v_{0}g+F_{0}(f)).
Proof.

The proof follows from Theorem 3.20, Theorem 4.9 and Remark 4.10. More explicitly, DD is triangularizable if and only if there exists a decomposition

φ=τ1∘θ∘τ0∘α,\varphi=\tau_{1}\circ\theta\circ\tau_{0}\circ\alpha,

where φ∈Aut⁡(k⁡[x,y,z])\varphi\in{\rm Aut}(k[x,y,z]) and τ0,τ1∈T2​(k⁡(x))\tau_{0},\tau_{1}\in{\rm T}_{2}(k(x)). Denote α⁡(y)=f⁡(y,z)\alpha(y)=f(y,z), α⁡(z)=g⁡(y,z)\alpha(z)=g(y,z), where f,g∈k​(x)​[y,z]f,g\in k(x)[y,z]. Let

τ0:(yz)→(u0​yv0​z+F0​(y)),τ1:(yz)→(u1​yv1​z+F1​(y)).\tau_{0}\colon\begin{pmatrix}y\\ z\end{pmatrix}\rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}y\\ v_{0}z+F_{0}(y)\end{pmatrix},\qquad\tau_{1}\colon\begin{pmatrix}y\\ z\end{pmatrix}\rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}u_{1}y\\ v_{1}z+F_{1}(y)\end{pmatrix}.

Here ui,vi∈k⁡(x)u_{i},v_{i}\in k(x), Fi∈k​(x)[1]F_{i}\in k(x)^{[1]} for i=0,1i=0,1. Then

τ1∘θ∘τ0∘α:(yz)→(u1​(v0​g+F0​(f))v1​u0​f+F1​(v0​g+F0​(f))).\tau_{1}\circ\theta\circ\tau_{0}\circ\alpha\colon\begin{pmatrix}y\\ z\end{pmatrix}\rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}u_{1}(v_{0}g+F_{0}(f))\\ v_{1}u_{0}f+F_{1}\left(v_{0}g+F_{0}(f)\right)\end{pmatrix}.

If DD is triangularizable, then there exists an k⁡[x]k[x]-automorphism of k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z] of this form. By suitably choosing u1u_{1} and v0v_{0}, one can further assume f,g∈k⁡[x,y,z]f,g\in k[x,y,z] in the expression u1​(v0​g+F0​(f))u_{1}(v_{0}g+F_{0}(f)). ∎

It turns out that in many cases, the polynomial u1​(v0​g+F0​(f))u_{1}(v_{0}g+F_{0}(f)) cannot be the image of yy under any k⁡[x]k[x]-automorphism of k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z]. Let us fix two non-negative integers pp and qq not both zero. Let us consider the ℤ\mathbb{Z}-grading on k​(x)​[y,z]k(x)[y,z] given by deg⁡y=p\deg y=p, deg⁡z=q\deg z=q. If h∈k​(x)​[y,z]h\in k(x)[y,z], we denote by h¯\overline{h} the sum of terms with the biggest degree with respect to this grading. Since h¯\overline{h} is homogeneous, by deg⁡(h¯)\deg(\overline{h}), we mean the degree of any its terms. We denote the sum of linear terms of hh by L⁡(h)L(h).

Definition 4.12.

Let h∈k⁡[x,y,z]h\in k[x,y,z]. Denote the greatest common divisor of all coefficients in k⁡[x]k[x] of this polynomial, considered as polynomial in yy and zz, by d⁡(h)d(h). We say that a polynomial hh is primitive if d⁡(h)=1d(h)=1.

Proposition 4.13.

Let f,g∈k⁡[x,y,z]f,g\in k[x,y,z]. Suppose, gcd⁡(d⁡(L⁡(f)),d⁡(L⁡(g)))∈k⁡[x]∖k\gcd(d(L(f)),d(L(g)))\in k[x]\setminus k. Suppose, gg is a primitive polynomial such that g⁡(x,0,0)=0g(x,0,0)=0. Assume there exist non-negative integers pp and qq such that (p,q)≠(0,0)(p,q)\neq(0,0), f¯\overline{f} is primitive and deg⁡(f¯)>deg⁡(g¯)\deg(\overline{f})>\deg(\overline{g}). Then there does not exist any k⁡[x]k[x]-automorphism ζ\zeta of k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z], such that ζ⁡(y)=u1​(v0​g+F0​(f))\zeta(y)=u_{1}(v_{0}g+F_{0}(f)) for any u1,v0∈k⁡(x)u_{1},v_{0}\in k(x) and F0∈k⁡(x)​[t]=k​(x)[1]F_{0}\in k(x)[t]=k(x)^{[1]}.

Proof.

Suppose that, ζ\zeta is a k⁡[x]k[x]-automorphism of k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z], such that ζ⁡(y)=u1​(v0​g+F0​(f))\zeta(y)=u_{1}(v_{0}g+F_{0}(f)) for some u1,v0∈k⁡(x)u_{1},v_{0}\in k(x) and F0∈k​(x)​[t]F_{0}\in k(x)[t]. Denote

u1​F0​[t]=an​tn+…+a0,where​ai∈k⁡(x),0⩽i⩽n.u_{1}F_{0}[t]=a_{n}t^{n}+\ldots+a_{0},\qquad\text{where}~a_{i}\in k(x),~0\leqslant i\leqslant n.

Let us show that ai∈k⁡[x]a_{i}\in k[x] for all i⩾0i\geqslant 0. If it’s not the case, we can define

m:=m​a​x​{i|ai∉k⁡[x]}.m:=max~\{i~|~a_{i}\notin k[x]\}.

Then terms of degree m​deg⁡(f¯)m\deg(\overline{f}) in ζ⁡(y)\zeta(y) coincide with terms of degree m​deg⁡(f¯)m\deg(\overline{f}) in u1​F0​(f)u_{1}F_{0}(f). Since for all j>mj>m, aj∈k⁡[x]a_{j}\in k[x] and f¯\overline{f} is primitive, sum of terms of degree m​deg⁡(f¯)m\deg(\overline{f}) in u1​F0​(f)u_{1}F_{0}(f) does not lie in k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z]. Therefore, all aia_{i} are in k⁡[x]k[x]. So u1​v0​gu_{1}v_{0}g in k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z]. Since gg is primitive, u1​v0∈k⁡[x]u_{1}v_{0}\in k[x]. Hence, gcd⁡(d⁡(L⁡(a1​f)),d⁡(L⁡(u1​v0​g)))∉k\gcd(d(L(a_{1}f)),d(L(u_{1}v_{0}g)))\notin k. As a result, the ideal

(∂ζ⁡(y)∂y,∂ζ⁡(y)∂z)⊲k⁡[x,y,z]\Big(\dfrac{\partial\zeta(y)}{\partial y},\dfrac{\partial\zeta(y)}{\partial z}\Big)\triangleleft k[x,y,z]

is proper. So we have a contradiction. ∎

Example 4.14.

Let us fix non-zero polynomials r1,r2∈k⁡[x]r_{1},r_{2}\in k[x] and h1,h2∈k⁡[x,t]h_{1},h_{2}\in k[x,t] such that

  • •

5 Rank 𝟑\mathbf{3} derivations

In [18], Freudenburg introduced the following example of a rank​ 3\mathrm{rank}\,3 derivation Δ\Delta of B=k⁡[x,y,z]B=k[x,y,z]. Denote

u=x​z−y2​and​v=z​u2+2​x2​y​u+x5.u=xz-y^{2}~~\text{and}~~v=zu^{2}+2x^{2}yu+x^{5}.

Then Δ=Jac(u,v,⋅).\Delta={\rm Jac}(u,v,\cdot). The proof that Δ\Delta has rank 3 is based on the fact that Δ\Delta is homogeneous with respect to the standard ℤ\mathbb{Z}-grading. Till now, all known rank 33 derivations are ℤ\mathbb{Z}-homogeneous for suitable ℤ\mathbb{Z}-gradings. In this section, we give a new proof of the fact that Δ\Delta has rank 3. This proof does not use the homogeneity of Δ\Delta. Moreover, we prove a sufficient condition for an LND obtained by local slice construction to be of rank 3. This approach allows us to give new examples of rank 33 LNDs, which are not homogeneous. In particular, we construct a family of rank 33 LNDs, of which Δ\Delta is a member.

We begin with an elementary lemma.

Lemma 5.1.

Let B=k[3]B=k^{[3]}, D(≠0)∈LND⁡(B)D(\neq 0)\in{\rm LND}(B) and A:=Ker​DA:={\rm Ker}~D. Let gg be a local slice of DD and let D⁡(g)=f∈AD(g)=f\ \in A. Then A⁡[g]A[g] is DD-invariant and the restriction of DD to A⁡[g]A[g] equals f​∂∂g∈LND⁡(A⁡[g])f\dfrac{\partial}{\partial g}\in{\rm LND}(A[g]).

Proof.

Let A=k⁡[u,v](=k[2])A=k[u,v](=k^{[2]}). Let δ=f​∂∂g\delta=f\dfrac{\partial}{\partial g}. Then δ⁡(u)=δ⁡(v)=0\delta(u)=\delta(v)=0 and δ⁡(g)=f\delta(g)=f. So D|A⁡[g]=δ∈LND⁡(A⁡[g])D|_{A[g]}=\delta\in{\rm LND}(A[g]). Since gg is a local slice of DD, we have k⁡[x,y,z,1f]=k⁡[u,v,1f]​[g]k[x,y,z,\frac{1}{f}]=k[u,v,\frac{1}{f}][g]. So any element s∈Bs\in B can be represented as

s=fs​(u,v,g)fms,where​fs∈k⁡[u,v,g]=A⁡[g]​and​ms∈ℕ∪{0}.s=\dfrac{f_{s}(u,v,g)}{f^{m_{s}}},~\text{where}~f_{s}\in k[u,v,g]=A[g]~\text{and}~m_{s}\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}.

One can extend δ\delta to BB by defining δ⁡(s):=δ⁡(fs)fms\delta(s):=\dfrac{\delta(f_{s})}{f^{m_{s}}}. Then

fms​δ​(s)=δ⁡(fs​(u,v,g))=f​∂fs∂g=fms​D​(s).f^{m_{s}}{\delta}(s)=\delta(f_{s}(u,v,g))=f\dfrac{\partial f_{s}}{\partial g}=f^{m_{s}}D(s).

So δ=D\delta=D in BB. ∎

Remark 5.2.

In notations as above, DD admits a non-equivalent LND EE of BB commuting with DD if and only if δ=D|A⁡[g]\delta=D|_{A[g]} admits a non-equivalent LND ξ\xi of A⁡[g]A[g]. Indeed, ff generates both plinth ideals pl⁡(D)\mathrm{pl}(D) and pl⁡(δ)\mathrm{pl}(\delta). Then Proposition 4.1 implies the goal.

Thus we have the following result.

Proposition 5.3.

Let B=k[3]B=k^{[3]}, D(≠0)∈LND⁡(B)D(\neq 0)\in{\rm LND}(B) be of rank 33 and A:=Ker​DA:={\rm Ker}~D. Then if gg is any minimal local slice of DD, then D⁡(g)D(g) cannot be written as an univariate polynomial in any variable of AA.

Proof.

Suppose the converse. Then there exists x∈Ax\in A such that A=k​[x][1]A=k[x]^{[1]} and D⁡(g)∈k⁡[x]D(g)\in k[x]. By Lemma 2.15 (ii), xx is a variable in BB and since rk​D=3\rm{rk}~D=3, we have a contradiction. ∎

Lemma 5.1 and Proposition 5.3 imply that DD is an extension of rank 1 derivation f​∂∂gf\frac{\partial}{\partial g} on A⁡[g]A[g], where f=D⁡(g)∈Af=D(g)\in A cannot be written as an univariate polynomial in any variable of AA. Note that similar extension we obtain considering any slice hh of DD. Indeed, since D⁡(h)D(h) is divisible by f=D⁡(g)f=D(g), it cannot be written as an univariate polynomial in any variable of AA. If DD is irreducible, the converse of Proposition 5.3 is true. So we obtain the following statement.

Proposition 5.4.

Let B=k[3]B=k^{[3]} and DD be an irreducible LND of BB. Put A=Ker​DA=\mathrm{Ker}\,D. Let gg be a minimal local slice of DD. Suppose D⁡(g)D(g) cannot be written as an univariate polynomial in any variable of AA. Then rk​D=3\mathrm{rk}\,D=3.

Assume that DD is irreducible of rank at most 22, by Lemma 4.3, there exists g~∈B\tilde{g}\in B and a variable xx of BB in AA such that D⁡(g~)∈k⁡[x]D(\tilde{g})\in k[x]. Let gg be any minimal local slice of DD. Then D⁡(g)|D⁡(g~)D(g)\mid D(\tilde{g}). Hence D⁡(g)D(g) is a univariate polynomial in xx, which by Lemma 2.15 (i) is also a variable in AA. ∎

Using the assertions above we obtain the following criterion for an irreducible derivation DD of k[3]k^{[3]} to be an LND of rank 3.

Theorem 5.5.

Let B=k⁡[x,y,z]B=k[x,y,z] and DD be an irreducible derivation of BB. Then DD is an LND of rank 3 if and only if there are polynomials f,h,r∈Bf,h,r\in B such that

    Ker​D=k⁡[f,h]\mathrm{Ker}\,D=k[f,h];

  3. (iii)

    there are no such p,q,l∈k⁡[f,h]p,q,l\in k[f,h] and s∈Bs\in B, that r−p=s​qr-p=sq, v=q​lv=ql, and q∉kq\notin k;

    x,y,z∈k⁡[f,h,r,1v]x,y,z\in k[f,h,r,\frac{1}{v}].

Suppose that the conditions (i)-(iv) hold. Then DD is an LND. Indeed, D⁡(f)=D⁡(h)=D⁡(v)=0D(f)=D(h)=D(v)=0 and D⁡(r)∈k⁡[f,h]D(r)\in k[f,h]. Since v∈pl⁡(D)=(l)v\in\mathrm{pl}(D)=(l), there exists q∈Aq\in A, such that v=q​lv=ql. Therefore, D⁡(r−s​q)=v−l​q=0D(r-sq)=v-lq=0. So, r−s​q=p∈Ar-sq=p\in A. By (iii), q∈k∗q\in k^{*}. This contradicts that l∈pl⁡(D)=(v)l\in\mathrm{pl}(D)=(v). By Proposition 2.6, x,y,z∈k⁡[f,h,r,1v]x,y,z\in k[f,h,r,\frac{1}{v}]. ∎

The following corollary gives sufficient conditions for a LND of k[3]k^{[3]} obtained by a local slice construction to be of rank 33.

∎

So we see that Freudenburg’s example can be considered as a member of a large family of rank 33 LNDs on k[3]k^{[3]}.
